- Daemon-Fault-Tolerance.md: describe the actual worker heartbeat relay path
  and the ephemeral-znode supervisor liveness mechanism.
- Lifecycle-of-a-topology.md: note (inline in the 0.7.1 walkthrough) that the
  ZK-directory heartbeat model was replaced in 2.0.
- Cluster-State-Serialization.md: clarify worker heartbeats are not persisted
  in ZooKeeper by default (only under Pacemaker/legacy configuration).

  supervisor timeout check exists, so nimbus.supervisor.timeout.secs is never

Add storm-iceberg module: an Apache Iceberg sink bolt (#8950)

* Add storm-iceberg Trident sink

New external module writing Trident batches to Apache Iceberg tables
directly from a topology, with exactly-once semantics.

Each batch is committed in a single Iceberg transaction that atomically
appends the data files and records the transaction id in the table
property storm.trident.<topologyName>.<partitionIndex>.last-committed-txid,
so replayed batches are detected and skipped even across worker crashes
and commits whose outcome was unknown to the writer.

Includes:
- IcebergOptions: catalog properties passed verbatim to Iceberg's
  CatalogUtil.buildIcebergCatalog, so any catalog works with its
  standard keys; file format, target file size and table auto-creation.
- RecordMapper with a field-name based default doing the standard
  primitive conversions; required columns without a value fail loudly.
- Partitioned tables through Iceberg's fanout writer, one open data file
  per partition.
- Per-batch table refresh, so schema and partition spec evolution is
  picked up without restarting the workers.
- Metrics-v2 instrumentation: records written, data files and bytes
  committed, commit latency, commit failures, skipped replays.
- A shutdown hook releasing the catalog client, since Trident's State
  has no lifecycle callback.
- Documentation and two runnable example topologies, unpartitioned and
  partitioned.

* Fix small files problems in apache iceberg ingestion. Estimate bytes ingested per commit.

* Fix examples iceberg (shuffling and max batches pending)

* Add BoundedTupleSpout

* Move to IcebergBolt implementation

* Add dependency management in root pom for a single point of check

The Iceberg version was pinned in the module's own properties, where a
project-wide dependency bump would not see it. It now lives in the root
pom alongside hadoop.version, with the artifacts managed in
dependencyManagement; storm-iceberg declares them without versions.

This does not widen the dependency's reach. dependencyManagement fixes
versions without adding dependencies, so modules that do not declare
Iceberg still resolve none of it: storm-client and storm-server both
show zero Iceberg artifacts. The direction also prevents it, since
storm-iceberg depends on storm-client (provided) and nothing in core
depends on storm-iceberg.

Neither binary distribution bundles it either: like every other
external/* connector, storm-iceberg ships only its README in both the
full and the lite assembly, so Iceberg reaches only topologies that ask
for it.

The catalog implementations (iceberg-aws, -gcp, -hive, -nessie, ...) are
deliberately absent from the managed set: they are supplied by the
topology rather than pulled in transitively.

* Add a split writer/committer sink to storm-iceberg

IcebergBolt writes and commits in the same task, so a sink at parallelism N
committing every T seconds produces N/T snapshots per second, each a metadata
rewrite plus a compare-and-swap on the catalog. Past a certain parallelism the
only way to keep that load down is to commit less often, which is to say to
accept more latency.

IcebergWriterBolt and IcebergCommitterBolt break that coupling. Writers seal
batches on the same thresholds IcebergBolt uses, but instead of committing they
emit one descriptor tuple carrying the batch's data files, anchored to every
tuple of the batch, and then ack those tuples. Anchoring preserves the
guarantee: acking an input after emitting an anchored child does not close the
spout tuple's ack tree, so the source advances only once the descriptor is
acked by the committer. A single committer accumulates descriptors and appends
them in one Iceberg commit, so snapshot rate is set by the group-commit cadence
rather than by writer parallelism.

Measured on a 6-way sink at a 10 s cadence: 115 snapshots with IcebergBolt
against 20 with the split sink, for the same 360k rows, the same 115 data
files and the same visibility latency (p50 5,454 ms against 5,506 ms).

Supporting changes:

- DataFileCodec is extracted from CommitWal, since the descriptor tuples and
  the WAL now share one data-file serialisation.
- The commit WAL is keyed by component and task index rather than task id, so
  a writer and a committer in the same topology cannot collide and a recovered
  task finds its own entries.
- IcebergOptions gains group-commit thresholds (interval and max data files)
  and a per-component tick interval, so writer and committer can be paced
  independently.
- Seal metrics and pending-commit gauges, so a stalled committer is visible.
- Pending state stays visible for the duration of a commit, and write errors
  fail fast rather than being deferred to the seal.
- A split-sink example topology, with both shapes documented.

* Harden storm-iceberg failure paths and simplify commit recovery

Apply worker file ownership and mode via an open descriptor (#9006)

* Apply worker file ownership and mode via an open descriptor

setup_permissions() opens each entry with O_NOFOLLOW, confirms via fstat
that it is still the same object fts_read() classified (matching device
and inode), and uses fchown/fchmod on that descriptor instead of lchown/
chmod by pathname.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Open worker tree entries with O_NONBLOCK to avoid blocking on a swapped FIFO

O_NOFOLLOW rejects a symlink but not a FIFO, so if an entry is replaced by a
FIFO between fts_read() classifying it and the open, open(O_RDONLY) would block
the launcher. O_NONBLOCK avoids that; it is a no-op for regular files and
directories, and the fstat device/inode check still rejects the swapped object.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Pin org.jspecify:jspecify so the daemon and worker classpaths agree

Apply one redaction rule to configuration served and logged by Storm (#9069)

* Apply one redaction rule to configuration served by the Nimbus API

Nimbus hands configuration to clients from more than one operation, and the
treatment differed between them. getNimbusConf and getTopologyConf redact
credential values before returning them. getTopologyPageInfo did not, and it
serves the daemon configuration merged with the topology configuration, so it
returned strictly more than either of the other two.

Route both topology-facing operations through a single helper so the rule is
the same wherever Nimbus serializes a configuration map for a client:

- getTopologyPageInfo masks before serializing into
  TopologyPageInfo.topology_conf, which the UI renders as the "configuration"
  field of the topology page and of the metrics response.
- getTopologyConf moves from maskPasswords to maskCredentials. That
  additionally covers keys no annotated field declares, since plugins read
  their own keys straight out of the map, so an operator-supplied password
  key in a topology configuration is covered too.
- The Blowfish tuple serializer key is handled inside the helper rather than
  repeated at each call site. Its constant lives outside the config classes,
  so the annotation scan cannot see it, and its name matches no credential
  pattern.

Masking applies to the copy that gets serialized. The daemon's own
configuration and the stored topology configuration are left alone, and
workers continue to read real values from the blobstore-distributed
configuration rather than from these responses.

The only consumers of TopologyPageInfo.topology_conf are the two UI display
paths in UIHelpers, so no functional reader loses a value it depends on.

* Stop logging configuration values that carry credentials

Seven sites wrote a configuration map, or an object that stringifies one,
straight into a log:

- RedisKeyValueStateProvider logged the full merged worker configuration on
  its error path. Worker masks that same map two frames away.
- CommonKafkaSpoutConfig.toString appended every Kafka property value.
  KafkaSpoutConfig already overrode it without them, so only the Trident
  spouts, which inherit the base, were affected.
- KafkaBolt.toString appended the producer properties.
- HdfsSpout logged each HDFS configuration override value.
- TopologySpoutLag logged the whole component configuration.
- ResourceUtils trace-logged the component json_conf, for bolts and spouts.
- StormSubmitter logged the serialized topology configuration.

Where the credential name pattern is enough, the value is masked. Where it is
not -- sasl.jaas.config matches neither the annotation set nor the pattern --
the log now names the keys instead of their values, which is what these lines
were diagnostically useful for anyway.

Also corrects the "proerties" spelling in KafkaBolt.toString.

Drop malformed tuple payloads instead of killing the receiving worker (#9076)

* Drop malformed tuple payloads instead of killing the receiving worker

A tuple payload that cannot be decoded escaped recv() into the Netty fatal
handler, terminating the worker. The supervisor restarted the worker, and the
same poison message terminated it again.

recv() now catches per-message deserialization failures whose cause chain
contains one of the exceptions raised by undecodable payloads (IOException,
KryoException, IllegalArgumentException, NegativeArraySizeException,
ClassCastException, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, BufferUnderflowException,
NullPointerException, ClassNotFoundException). The offending message is
dropped, the failure is logged with the destination task and payload size,
the count is exposed as a deserializationFailures metric next to the message
size metrics, and the rest of the batch is delivered. Any other Exception
still propagates unchanged, and Errors are not caught.

https://github.com/apache/storm/issues/9074

* Rate-limit drop logging and report deserializationFailures from the server

A topology stuck receiving poison payloads would flood the worker log with
one ERROR per dropped message. recv() now logs the first 10 failures
individually, then one summary ERROR per 100 further failures carrying the
running total, in the WorkerState "Total Drop Count= {}" style. 1000
consecutive failures without a success log a single WARN pointing at a
persistent fault; any successful deserialization resets that counter.

NullPointerException stays outside the tolerated set: it usually signals a
bug rather than a malformed payload. The case a bad tuple could trigger,
an unknown source task, is rejected up front in KryoTupleDeserializer
with IllegalArgumentException naming the task; that lookup NPEd during
stream resolution before this change.

Server.getState() publishes deserializationFailures as a top-level key,
always present, including when it is 0, read through
getAndResetDeserializationFailures() on the callback. getValueAndReset()
reports only the size metrics, null when they are disabled.

isToleratedDeserializationFailure walks the exception cause chain once and
checks every tolerated type per frame, instead of once per type.

Tests inject a replacement deserializer through a package-private setter,
and a new ServerTest covers the top-level key.

https://github.com/apache/storm/issues/9074

* Narrow the recv() try to deserialization so post-decode failures propagate

Tuple addressing and the metrics update run after the tuple has decoded; a
failure there is not a deserialization failure and must not drop a decoded
tuple or inflate the count.

Harden the java serialization fallback bridge with a JEP-290 serial filter (#9075)

* Harden the java serialization fallback bridge with a JEP-290 serial filter

Add topology.fall.back.on.java.serialization.filter, a JEP-290 filter
pattern for the java serialization fallback bridge. DefaultKryoFactory
parses the pattern once at kryo construction, so an invalid pattern
fails worker setup with the config key in the error, and
SerializableSerializer installs it via setObjectInputFilter whenever it
deserializes. The filter is topology-scoped and also covers
programmatic construction such as local mode, which a JVM-wide
jdk.serialFilter in worker.childopts does not reach.

conf/defaults.yaml sets a default pattern: a deny-list of well-known
gadget namespaces (commons-collections 3/4 functors and comparators,
beanutils, xalan external and JDK-internal, rowset, c3p0, groovy
closures) plus maxbytes=10485760. An empty or unset value leaves the
bridge unfiltered, as before.

The pattern uses JEP-290 wildcards: pkg.* covers direct package members
and pkg.** also covers subpackages; tests exercise both depths against
loadable classes in denied packages, end to end through
KryoValuesSerializer and KryoValuesDeserializer.

* Rework the fallback serial filter: opt-in sample, merge, validation

Remove the default value of topology.fall.back.on.java.serialization.filter
from conf/defaults.yaml. A shipped deny-list is not a security boundary,
and defaulting it on silently replaced the operator's JVM-wide
jdk.serialFilter on the bridge streams. docs/SECURITY.md now carries a
sample pattern instead: the previous gadget deny-list plus well-known
additions (JMX reflection gadget, JNDI, RMI, Clojure, FileUpload,
BeanShell, Jython, JBoss). maxbytes alone would not bound a single
large primitive array, so the pattern also carries
maxdepth/maxrefs/maxarray.

SerializableSerializer now reads the stream's existing filter (a JVM-wide
jdk.serialFilter, if set) and merges the two via ObjectInputFilter.merge,
so a JVM-wide allow-list still applies on this path.

The bridge also validates the declared length before allocating: a
negative length is always refused, and on buffered input (the tuple
paths) a declared length larger than the bytes remaining in the frame
is refused before the byte[] allocation. Stream-backed programmatic
use keeps the previous behavior, since the stream may still deliver
the declared bytes.

KryoSerializableDefault takes the filter as a constructor argument and
holds it in a final field; the mutable setter is removed so the filter
cannot be swapped after construction.

ConfigValidation gains SerialFilterPatternValidator, wired to the
TOPOLOGY_FALL_BACK_ON_JAVA_SERIALIZATION_FILTER field, so a malformed
pattern fails topology submission with the key named; the parse error
in DefaultKryoFactory is now an IllegalArgumentException.

The filter applies to the default factory's fallback bridge; a custom
topology.kryo.factory or the pre-kryo state serializer is not covered.

Tests now use JDK classes only and cover wildcard depth, the sample
pattern, the size limits, the length guard, and the merge helper.

STORM-3871: sweep dependency blobs that outlive their topology's cleanup

A dependency blob key carries no topology id, so a blob that survives the
cleanup pass of its topology (a failed submission, or a blob that another
nimbus hands back to the leader after it was deleted) stays in the blob
store forever. doCleanup now also removes dependency blobs whose key is
provably unique to one topology once no topology has referred to them for
nimbus.inbox.jar.expiration.secs.

STORM-3871: stop a non-leader nimbus from registering a deleted blob again

The leader deletes a blob's zookeeper nodes one by one. A non-leader
that syncs in between downloads the blob from another nimbus and then
registers its copy after the key is gone, which registers the key as
new, and the other nimbus instances, the leader included, download the
blob back from it. Only the leader storing a blob a client uploads may
now register a key zookeeper does not know; any other nimbus gets a
KeyNotFoundException instead.

fix(napi): memory leak in PromiseRaw cleanup callback (#2995)

* fix(napi): fix memory leak in Promise::from_unknown()

This commit fixes a memory leak that occurred when converting a Promise
from an Unknown object, specifically manifesting in Deno environments.

The issue was in the `promise_callback_finalizer` function, which had
a type mismatch when cleaning up callback allocations:

1. The callback was stored as `Box<(Cb, *mut bool)>` (a tuple containing
   the callback and an executed flag pointer)
2. The finalizer incorrectly cast it as `Box<Cb>` when trying to free it
3. This caused improper deallocation and memory leaks

The fix ensures:
- The executed flag allocation is always properly cleaned up
- The callback tuple is cast to the correct type `(Cb, *mut bool)`
  before being dropped
- All allocations are properly freed in both execution paths (callback
  executed or not executed)

fix(napi): handle ThreadsafeFunction callback errors gracefully during shutdown (#3188)

When a Node.js environment is tearing down (e.g. Ctrl+C during watch mode
in a worker thread), NAPI calls can fail with unexpected status codes.

Reported in rolldown/rolldown#8951: pressing Ctrl+C while rolldown's watch
mode is performing its initial build causes a reproducible panic in napi-rs.

The panic occurs in `handle_call_js_cb_status` in the `else` branch, which
handles status codes that are neither `napi_ok` nor `napi_pending_exception`.
The full control flow is:

1. `call_js_cb` is the C callback invoked by Node's ThreadsafeFunction
   machinery on the main/JS thread.
2. It calls `napi_call_function` to invoke the JS callback, or
   `napi_fatal_exception` when the Rust callback errors.
3. The return status flows to `handle_call_js_cb_status(status, raw_env)`.
4. If status is `napi_pending_exception`, the function clears the exception
   and calls `napi_fatal_exception` — this path already tolerates
   `napi_pending_exception` as a return from `napi_fatal_exception`.
5. For any other non-ok status, the `else` branch constructs a JS Error
   object (via `napi_create_string_utf8` × 2 + `napi_create_error`) and
   calls `napi_fatal_exception`. Every one of these calls used `assert_eq!`
   against `napi_ok`, which panics during environment teardown.

During shutdown, `napi_fatal_exception` returns `napi_pending_exception`
(status 10) instead of `napi_ok`, and the string/error construction calls
can also fail. The fix:

- Replace `assert_eq!` with early returns on `napi_create_string_utf8` and
  `napi_create_error` — if we can't even construct the error object in a
  half-torn-down environment, there's nothing useful we can do.
- Tolerate `napi_pending_exception` from `napi_fatal_exception`, matching
  the pattern already used in the `napi_pending_exception` branch above.

fix(cli): respect --cross-compile when host matches target (#3189)

When --cross-compile / -x is passed, cargo-zigbuild should be used
regardless of whether host platform matches target. This allows pinning
a lower glibc version via zig's linker on native builds (e.g. building
x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu on ubuntu-latest with glibc 2.39 but targeting
glibc 2.28 for broader compatibility).

This was fixed in v2 by #1432 (fixing #1430) but the fix was not
carried over to the v3 CLI rewrite in #1492. The v3 code skipped
cargo-zigbuild when host platform/arch/abi matched the target, logging
a warning but silently falling through to cargo build, which links
against the host glibc.

Without this fix, NAPI-RS projects building linux-x64-gnu on
ubuntu-latest (glibc 2.39) produce binaries incompatible with systems
running glibc < 2.35, including Amazon Linux 2023 (glibc 2.34),
Vercel's build container, and RHEL 9.

feat(cli): opt-in runtime enum for #[napi(string_enum)] via --runtime-string-enum (#3284)

* fix(cli): emit runtime enum for string enums under --no-const-enum

Fixes #3283.

Numeric enums emitted `export declare enum X { ... }` under
`--no-const-enum`, but string enums emitted `export type X = 'A' | 'B'`
(type-only union) — blocking `MyEnum.Foo` access at the type level
even though `nativeBinding.X.Foo` worked at runtime.

Make the StringEnum branch share Enum's body via fall-through; only
the keyword (`enum` vs `const enum`) differs. No Rust-side changes
needed — napi-rs's enum codegen already registers runtime values
identically for numeric and string enums.

The runtime-enum form does not hit the TS1254 constraint that
blocked #2054's `as const` approach, as the numeric-enum branch
already demonstrates.

The existing `noConstEnum` snapshot test fixture had no string-enum
entries, so this codepath had zero test coverage. Added a `Status`
string-enum entry to the fixture and updated the snapshot.

* feat(cli): make runtime-enum string-enum emission opt-in via --runtime-string-enum

The previous commit flipped `#[napi(string_enum)]` under
`--no-const-enum` from a type-only union to a runtime enum
(`export declare enum X { ... }`). That's a TS assignability break
for consumers using bare-literal patterns: `const x: X = "Foo"` is
assignable to `'Foo' | 'Bar'` but not to `enum X { Foo = 'Foo' }`.

Make the runtime-enum emission opt-in via `--runtime-string-enum`
(or `runtimeStringEnum` in `napi.json`). Default reverts to the
type-only union — existing consumers keep working unchanged;
consumers who want member access (`X.Foo`) opt in explicitly.

  - cli/src/def/build.ts: new `--runtime-string-enum` Option +
    pass-through + type field.
  - cli/src/api/build.ts: forward through `generateTypeDef`.
  - cli/src/utils/config.ts: new `runtimeStringEnum` field on
    `UserNapiConfig` (configurable via napi.json).
  - cli/src/utils/typegen.ts: split the `Enum`/`StringEnum` case
    fall-through into a three-way branch in `StringEnum` —
    `constEnum` always wins; `runtimeStringEnum` flips the
    `--no-const-enum` path from union to runtime enum.
  - cli/src/utils/__tests__/typegen.spec.ts: two new snapshot
    tests for the additional combinations (`constEnum=false +
    runtimeStringEnum=true`, and `constEnum=true +
    runtimeStringEnum=true` no-op).

Reverting this commit restores the always-runtime-enum behavior
from the previous one — useful if a future major considers a
default flip.

fix(cli): NAPI_RS_FORCE_WASI only activates on 'true' or 'error' (#3236)

The generated native.js template treated process.env.NAPI_RS_FORCE_WASI as a
plain truthy-string check. In JavaScript any non-empty string is truthy,
including 'false' and '0', so setting NAPI_RS_FORCE_WASI=false (intending
to opt out of forced WASI) inadvertently triggered the WASI fallback — the
same path that tries to load <pkg>.wasi.cjs and fails with ENOENT for
packages that don't ship a WASI binding.

Reported by lancedb/lancedb#3267, where downstream users hit:

  ENOENT: no such file or directory, open '.../@lancedb/lancedb/dist/lancedb.wasi.cjs'

This patch extracts a single `forceWasi` boolean at the top of the
generated script (equal to 'true' or 'error') and uses it consistently
at the four call sites that previously did a truthy-string check. The
existing `=== 'error'` branch at the bottom is preserved unchanged — it
already did the right thing.

This is a template change, so the fix is picked up the next time a
downstream package runs `napi build`. No behavior change for
existing users who had NAPI_RS_FORCE_WASI unset or set to 'true'/'error'.

Related: PR #2919 added the 'error' tri-state; this patch completes
the tri-state handling by making the other two values ('true' and
everything-else) behave as documented.

fix(napi): unify Reference finalize callbacks on Arc (Rc/Arc type confusion) (#3313)

The `finalize_callbacks` allocation backing `Reference<T>` was created with
`Rc::into_raw` (callback_info.rs `_construct`/`_factory`, class.rs) and
reclaimed with `Rc::from_raw` in the GC finalizer (mod.rs), yet reconstructed
with `Arc::from_raw` in `Reference::from_value_ptr` and `add_ref`
(value_ref.rs). Since #2668 changed the `Reference` field to `Arc<Cell<..>>`
and added `unsafe impl Sync`, the same heap allocation was being used as both
`Rc` and `Arc` — undefined behavior: mismatched `RcBox`/`ArcInner` layout
assumptions, mixed atomic/non-atomic refcount access, and a deallocation path
that assumes `ArcInner` for an `RcBox` allocation. The reported impact is a
process abort (DoS) under repeated `Reference<T>` conversions plus GC.

Reverting to `Rc` is unsound because `Reference`'s `unsafe impl Sync` requires
atomic refcounting. This completes the #2668 refactor by switching the three
allocation sites and the finalizer to `Arc`. The `#[allow(clippy::
arc_with_non_send_sync)]` matches the existing precedent in
threadsafe_function.rs: the inner `Cell` is only mutated on the JS thread via
`Env`, as documented on `Reference`.

Reported-by: Thanasis Trispiotis

fix(napi): ReadableStream Reader loses chunks and aborts on errored streams (#3328)

* fix(napi): prevent lost chunks and process abort in ReadableStream Reader

Two ship-blocking bugs in the ReadableStream `Reader` (read.rs):

1. Lost chunks on multi-chunk streams. `poll_next` issued a JS `read()` on
   every poll with no "read already in flight" guard, storing results into a
   single slot. Under a fast producer two reads could be in flight and the
   second overwrote the first, silently dropping a chunk and producing a wrong
   result. Replace the `(RwLock<Result<Option<T>>>, AtomicBool)` state with a
   single `std::sync::Mutex<ReaderInner<T>>` that serializes drain/issue/store,
   keeping at most one read outstanding and storing the latest waker in shared
   state (woken from `finally`). Buffered errors are now surfaced via
   `Poll::Ready(Some(Err(_)))`, and `catch` marks the stream done so no further
   reads are issued after an error.

2. Process abort on errored streams. The `.catch` branch created the error
   reference with `napi_create_reference(..., 0, ...)` (refcount 0); the consume
   path unrefs it exactly once, and unref of a 0-count reference fails a
   debug_assert, aborting the whole process instead of rejecting the Promise.
   Create the reference with refcount 1.

* fix(napi): convert ReadableStream read rejections to owned errors

The Reader's promise `catch` previously captured the JS rejection value in
a napi reference and stored it inside the `Error` returned from
`poll_next`. Because `Reader<T>` is a `Send` `futures::Stream`, a consumer
can drop that `Err` on a runtime thread, where `Error::drop` would release
the napi reference off the JS thread — aborting the process / UB. This
affects every napi `ReadableStream` consumer on a rejection.

Extract the error message into an owned Rust `Error` (no `napi_ref`) on the
JS thread inside `catch`, so the yielded `Err` is safe to move to and drop
on any thread. As a bonus the rejection now carries the JS error's message
instead of an empty reason.

perf(napi): outline non-generic core of ThreadsafeFunction::create (#3334)

* perf(napi): outline non-generic core of ThreadsafeFunction::create

`ThreadsafeFunction::create` is generic over
`<T, Return, CallJsBackArgs, ErrorStatus, ...>`, but almost its entire
body — the async resource name creation, the
`napi_create_threadsafe_function` call and the weak-ref handling — is
type-independent. The same FFI setup is therefore monomorphized once per
distinct callback signature, which adds up quickly for addons that
register many threadsafe functions.

Extract that type-independent work into a non-generic `create_raw`
helper. The generic `create` becomes a thin shell that boxes the user
callback and forwards the two `extern "C"` trampolines plus the raw
callback pointer. The public API, the runtime behavior and the generated
FFI calls are unchanged.

Measured on rolldown (a heavy napi consumer with ~42 distinct
threadsafe-function instantiations) through a local `[patch.crates-io]`:

- `ThreadsafeFunction::create` LLVM IR: 12,768 -> 2,058 lines (-84%)
- `napi` crate `.text` in the built addon: 492.1 KiB -> 468.0 KiB (-24 KiB)

* fix(napi): reclaim boxed callback when ThreadsafeFunction::create_raw fails

Outlining the FFI core moved `Box::into_raw(callback)` ahead of the async
resource name creation. If that string creation (or the
`napi_create_threadsafe_function` call itself) fails inside `create_raw`,
N-API never takes ownership of the box and `thread_finalize_cb` is never
registered to reclaim it, so the callback closure and its captures leak.

Reclaim the box on any `create_raw` error in the generic `create` shell,
which is the only place that knows the concrete callback type. This also
closes the pre-existing leak on the `napi_create_threadsafe_function`
failure path.

* fix(napi): release Error's exception reference via the custom GC when dropped off-thread

An Error created from a JS exception (From<Unknown> — the Promise-rejection
path — or a ThreadsafeFunction JS-throw in call_js_cb) owns a napi_ref to
the JS error object. Error is Send, but Drop released that reference with
napi_reference_unref/napi_delete_reference on whatever thread ran it;
dropping such an Error off the owning JS thread mutates V8's GlobalHandles
from a foreign thread and corrupts it (fatal
'Check failed: object_ != kGlobalHandleZapValue' /
'node->IsInUse()' checks, or delayed segfaults in GlobalHandles
Destroy/Create at unrelated call sites). Promise rejections awaited off the
JS thread hit this with no way to avoid it from safe code, since the Error
materializes on the awaiting thread.

Fix: capture the owning env's CustomGcHandle when the reference is created
and route the release exactly like ArrayBuffer/TypedArray drops (#3357):
direct unref+delete when dropped on the owning JS thread; enqueue on the
custom-GC TSFN when dropped anywhere else; safe leak once the env is gone
(aborted). The custom_gc callback now deletes only when the refcount
reaches zero so try_clone'd Errors sharing one reference stay correct
(buffer refs are never shared, so their behavior is unchanged).

Resolves the Drop @TODO about Errors carrying references.

- error:reject:offthread — Promise rejections awaited on the async runtime,
  so the ref-carrying Error materializes and drops on a tokio worker;
- error:clone:threads — try_clone siblings dropped on different threads
  (delete only at refcount zero);
- stash:error:teardown — Errors stashed in a worker-thread thread_local,
  dropped after env teardown (aborted/leak path).

Without the fix these crash deterministically with
'Check failed: object_ != kGlobalHandleZapValue' in napi_reference_unref
(verified by reverting crates/napi/src to napi-v3.10.0 and rerunning);
with it the full examples suite passes (223 tests, snapshot updated for

current thread unconditionally. Off the owning JS thread that increment

fix(napi): keep message and cause when cloning a JS-exception Error off-thread (#3373)

#3370 made `Error::try_clone()` return an `Err` placeholder ("Error holding a
JS exception reference can only be cloned on the thread that owns it") whenever
a JS-exception-backed `Error` was cloned off the owning JS thread. rolldown
clones build-worker errors off-thread via `try_clone().unwrap_or_else(|e| e)`,
so that placeholder replaced the real plugin messages (e.g. "load error"),
failing 16 error tests across 3 files in its CI after the patch release.

`try_clone` now touches the thread-affine `napi_ref` only with proof of
ownership (a napi4 custom-GC handle owned by the current thread). In every
other case — off the owning thread, no handle, or an error that holds no
reference — it returns a reference-less clone that preserves `status`,
`reason`, and the recursively cloned `cause` chain, which `into_value` rebuilds
into a fresh JS error. The owning-thread ref-sharing clone also carries a
reference-less cause backup so a later off-thread re-clone keeps the chain.
`throw_into` now only skips re-throwing when the env genuinely has a pending
exception, so a detached `PendingException` clone is surfaced instead of
silently swallowed.

Adds regression tests (off-thread message, off-thread cause, transitive cause,
detached pending exception) that pass on both native and wasm32-wasip1-threads.
Also makes a pre-existing #3370 wasm test robust to an emnapi environment
difference: a JS `null` cause is never reconstructed as a nested Error, but it
surfaces as nullish (`null` or `undefined` depending on the emnapi build) under
WASM, so the assertion now checks for nullish rather than one hardcoded value.

fix(napi): preserve the JS error object when cloning an Error off-thread (#3375)

#3373 made `Error::try_clone` off the owning JS thread return a
reference-less copy: it kept `status`/`reason`/`cause` but dropped the
original JS error object, so `into_value` rebuilt a bare `Error(reason)`
and lost `.stack`, the subclass, and arbitrary own properties. rolldown
clones plugin errors off a build worker and surfaces them on the JS
thread, so 5 error tests still failed (stack `at errorFn2`, the
`[plugin my-plugin]` decoration, and `e.errors[0]` props such as
`code`/`plugin`/`hook`).

Decouple the Rust-side clone count from napi's own reference refcount. The
three `Error` fields `maybe_raw`/`maybe_env`/`maybe_custom_gc` collapse into
one `maybe_ref: Option<Arc<ErrorRef>>`. `ErrorRef` owns the raw `napi_ref` +
`napi_env` + custom-GC handle and carries the release logic in
`impl Drop for ErrorRef` (the old `Error::drop` body); `Error`'s own `Drop`
is removed. `try_clone` shares the reference by cloning the `Arc` — an
atomic bump with zero napi FFI, so it is safe from any thread — instead of
calling `napi_reference_ref`. The single `napi_ref` is created at refcount
1, never ref/unref'd for cloning, and released exactly once by
`ErrorRef::drop` when the last `Arc` drops: directly on the owning JS
thread, or routed through the env's custom-GC TSFN when the last drop is
elsewhere.

Every reference read (`into_value`, `to_napi_value`, `create_error`,
deferred `into_rejected`) goes through a new `Error::referenced_value(env)`,
which returns the JS object only when `current_thread_owns_custom_gc` proves
it is safe on the current thread and returns `None` (rebuild from `reason`)
on a foreign env. Because `into_value` runs on the owning JS thread even
when `try_clone` ran off-thread, a carried reference yields the original
object with full fidelity.

* fix(napi): release FunctionRef off the JS thread via the custom-GC TSFN

thread — the same protocol `TypedArray`/`Buffer`/`Error` refs already use.

fans out rejecting streams with heap churn: it reliably SIGSEGVs before the fix

fix(napi): register the async runtime env cleanup hook per registration (#3400)

`napi_register_module_v1` runs once per env — the main thread, every
`worker_threads` worker (its own V8 isolate + env), and every Electron renderer
reload (env destroyed + recreated). Each call increments `MODULE_COUNT` and
starts the shared async runtime; teardown is refcounted by the `thread_cleanup`
env-cleanup hook, which decrements `MODULE_COUNT` and shuts the runtime down only
when it reaches zero (the last live env).

The hook was installed behind a process-wide one-shot gate
(`ENV_CLEANUP_HOOK_ADDED: RwLock<bool>`) that was set once and never reset, so it
registered for the first registration only. Every additional or recreated env
bumped `MODULE_COUNT` with no matching cleanup hook, so the count could never
return to zero and `shutdown_async_runtime` was never called — the runtime's
backend threads/tasks outlived the addon image (worker_threads, Electron reload).

Register the hook on every registration instead. The same addon can also be
(re)loaded into the *same* env (`unload.spec.js` clears the require cache and
re-`require`s it), and Node's `napi_add_env_cleanup_hook` asserts every
`(fn, arg)` pair is unique within an env — so each registration gets a distinct,
never-dereferenced cookie instead of a shared `null` arg. Otherwise the second
same-env load aborts in `AddEnvironmentCleanupHook` on `result.second`. One hook
per registration keeps `MODULE_COUNT` balanced (one decrement per increment), so
the last env's teardown still shuts the runtime down exactly once.

Split out of the #3352 review (codex, module_register.rs:577); the bug is
pre-existing on the `tokio_rt` path on `main`.

* fix(backend): derive class type tag from a process-unique static address

The TypeId-based tag had two real defects: `impl Hash for TypeId` hashes
only the lower 64 bits, capping entropy at 64 bits and letting distinct
classes with a colliding TypeId-half share a tag deterministically; and
TypeId is nominal, so two separately-compiled same-metadata addon builds
can share a TypeId, colliding across addons.

Derive the tag instead from the address of a per-class `AtomicU8` static.
The address is process-unique by construction (distinct classes have
distinct anchor statics; separately-loaded addons map statics at distinct
addresses) and is fed in injectively as the tag's lower half, so distinct
classes can never collide (no hashing, no birthday bound). AtomicU8 gives
the static interior mutability so it lands in writable data and the linker
never merges two classes' anchors. The body no longer names the class type,
so lifetime classes need no `'static` form for the tag.

fix(napi): guard JsDeferred against env teardown (#3404)

Guard `JsDeferred` so a deferred settling after (or while) its env tears down no longer calls into a freed threadsafe function and SIGABRTs (#2460).

A shared `Arc<DeferredHandle>` holds the pending threadsafe function behind a `Mutex<Option<..>>`: a settle takes it, an env cleanup hook abort-releases it on teardown, whichever locks first wins, and the lock is held across the FFI call so teardown cannot finalize the threadsafe function mid-settle. A `hook_registered` flag keeps the finalize callback from unregistering the env cleanup hook after the teardown drain already consumed it (Bun <= 1.2.20 aborts otherwise). `napi_resolve_deferred` returns early on the null-env teardown invocation.

Closes #2460

fix(napi): release JsDeferred tsfn on null-env teardown drain (#3404 follow-up) (#3408)

Follow-up hardening on top of #3404 (JsDeferred env-teardown guard).

- Fix a threadsafe-function leak on the null-env teardown drain. When a
  settle has already queued its `DeferredData` and the env tears down before
  the loop dispatches it, Node drains the leftover item with a null env. The
  early return skipped `napi_release_threadsafe_function`, so the queued item
  never discharged its owed thread-count release. Node's teardown delete is
  thread_count-gated on current versions (`Finalize` -> `MaybeDelete`, which
  keeps the object while `thread_count > 0`; only v22's `EmptyQueueAndDelete`
  deleted unconditionally), and emnapi behaves the same, so the threadsafe
  function leaked and accumulated across teardown races. Release it in the
  null-env branch too. Safe during the drain: `EmptyQueue` invokes the
  callback without holding the tsfn lock, and `state == kClosing` there, so
  `Release` drops the count and returns `napi_ok` without deleting — the
  following `MaybeDelete` performs the single delete.

- Make `JsDeferred::new` transactional. The threadsafe function is created
  before two more fallible steps (`napi_add_env_cleanup_hook` and, under the
  `deferred_trace` feature, `DeferredTrace::new`); a failure in either used to
  strand the ref'd tsfn (which keeps the event loop alive until env teardown)
  and, in one ordering, leak the trace `napi_ref` (`DeferredTrace` has no
  `Drop`). Create the trace ref last and release the tsfn on both error paths
  without freeing the boxed hook data (the tsfn finalize owns it).

- Correct the `hook_registered` doc: Bun aborts (`NAPI_PERISH`) on removing an
  unregistered cleanup-hook pair through 1.2.20, fixed in 1.2.21 (Bun #21883)
  to match Node's silent no-op — not "<= 1.2.18".

The filesystem-transaction journal captured file and parent dev/ino from a
non-bigint stat() and stored them as JSON numbers, then re-validated them on
recovery with Number.isSafeInteger. On Windows a 64-bit NTFS file reference
(ino) or volume serial (dev) frequently exceeds Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER, so the
non-bigint read is imprecise, Number.isSafeInteger returns false, and recovery
throws "Invalid file state in filesystem transaction journal" (flaky under the
400-file crash-recovery test on x86_64-pc-windows-msvc).

source (openFileSystemTransactionIdentity, snapshotFileSystemTransactionInput
source/destination, captureTransactionParentIdentity) and persist them as exact
decimal strings, and compare the parent identity with a bigint stat at both the
in-process (assertTransactionParentUnchanged) and recovery
(assertFileSystemTransactionJournalParentUnchanged) checks so capture and
compare share one representation. normalize now accepts either a decimal string
or an exact (safe, non-negative) number and canonicalises both to a string, so
existing numeric journals still recover while imprecise values are still
rejected rather than allowed to false-match a different inode. The mode field
and the reconciliation-lock identity subsystem are unchanged.

No journal version bump: the reader stays backward compatible (numeric journals
canonicalise to the same string form), which the v1/v2/v3 recovery fixtures
require, so nothing is mis-parsed.

journal+recover path (accept/round-trip and no-false-match), which fail against

* fix(cli): retire failed-snapshot leftovers by rename before deleting them

The failed-snapshot cleanup guard verified ownership with an lstat of the
destination pathname and then unlinked the same pathname — a TOCTOU window
the code itself documented as a known limitation: a successor swapped onto
the pathname between the two syscalls was deleted even though the
transaction never owned it.

Close the window with the subsystem's existing retire idiom
(retireExactFileSystemTransactionPath /
restoreUnexpectedFileSystemTransactionRetirement): atomically rename the
leftover to a unique process-private sibling, revalidate the retired entry
against the recorded 64-bit decimal-string identity, and unlink only a
revalidated match — the retired name is unreachable to other writers, so
the unlink deletes exactly the revalidated inode. A mismatched entry is
hard-linked back to the destination, or preserved at the retired name when
an even newer successor already reoccupied the pathname.

The race window is covered deterministically in tests through the
onBeforeRetire seam, which swaps a distinct inode onto the pathname between
the ownership pre-check and the retirement rename.

* test(runtime): never block in worker TLS destructors -- fixes the Windows loader-lock suite wedge

Root cause of the whole-suite silent Windows hang (runs 29195160953 and
86662331487; 20-minute Unit-tests step timeouts): the
multi_thread_shutdown_waits_for_worker_tls_destructors probe installed a

released it. On Windows, TLS destructors run inside LdrShutdownThread
while HOLDING the process loader lock. With two workers, the first
parked destructor held the loader lock, the second worker could not even
enter its own destructor (blocked acquiring the same lock), so the
release condition (both workers entered) was unsatisfiable: the first
worker parked forever with the loader lock held. From that instant every
thread::spawn and thread-exit in the process froze -- the other in-flight
tests wedged inside their own harness/pool spawns before any watchdog
existed (their bounds never armed), and with RUST_BACKTRACE=1 even the
panic path wedges (dbghelp DLL loading wants the same lock). That is why
four tests froze simultaneously with total silence in both runs. macOS
and Linux TSD destructors hold no process-global lock, which is why only
Windows hung; the wedge is not reproducible locally on macOS.

multi_thread_pending_timer_longer_than_park_deadline_does_not_panic --
the other two-run in-flight constant -- carries no independent wedge: it
installs no TLS state and its first acts are thread spawns (harness
runner, rayon pool), which is exactly where a held loader lock freezes
it; it is a dispatch-order-adjacent victim.

Fix (test layer; invariant preserved):
* WorkerTlsDropAction::Wait is replaced by Record { AtomicUsize }: the
  destructor only bumps a counter (loader-lock safe by construction).
  The invariant -- shutdown()'s worker retirement is a join barrier that
  includes TLS-destructor completion -- is now proven from outside: the
  shutdown thread samples the counter at the very instant shutdown()
  returns and asserts every worker had already recorded; a barrier that
  excluded destructors would race that sample and fail loudly.
* A LOADER-LOCK RULE comment at WorkerTlsDropAction documents that probe
  destructors may only record, never cross-thread wait.
* The two deadline-family tests whose thread-local hooks capture strong
  executor Arcs on an exiting runner thread now clear the hook slot
  right after block_on, before any assert can panic: a leftover hook
  dropped by a TLS destructor could otherwise drop the LAST executor Arc
  under the loader lock, and TimerHeap::drop joins the live timekeeper
  thread -- a join under the loader lock is the same deadlock.

Production audit (requested): no production TLS destructor or
thread-exit path waits on another thread. ACTIVE_RUNTIME_GENERATION,
ON_POOL_WORKER, ON_TIMER_THREAD, IN_SCHEDULER_DRIVER, BLOCKING_OWNER and
the dispatch counters are Cell<Copy> (no drop glue).
CURRENT_DEPENDENCY_STACK drop glue runs TaskDependency::drop, which only
takes its own exclusive state and drops a contained waiter -- no waits.
LIFO_SLOT drop glue would drop a stranded Runnable, but production
schedule closures capture WeakRuntimeExecutor, so no executor-drop
cascade is possible. RuntimeGenerationGuard::drop is a Cell store.

controller shutdown on ordinary threads, never from thread-exit context.

fix(napi-derive): keep the namespace when resolving cross-namespace type references (#3434)

* fix(backend): keep the namespace when resolving cross-namespace type references

CLASS_STRUCTS and ALIAS both map a Rust type's identifier to its bare
js_name, with no namespace attached. CLASS_STRUCTS is checked before
ALIAS/KNOWN_TYPES for any type path, so it's actually what resolves a
class reference in a function signature or struct field - and since it
only stores the bare name, a class declared in a namespace loses that
namespace the moment something else refers to it. Two classes in
different namespaces sharing a js_name make it worse: each is still
retrievable by its own Rust name, but both resolve to the same
unqualified string, which can't possibly be correct for both call
sites at once.

Store js_mod alongside js_name in CLASS_STRUCTS (behind a small
ClassStructRef so the one call site that wants the bare name for a
same-namespace self-reference - a factory method's return type - can
still ask for just that) and have add_alias qualify the alias text the
same way, since enums/consts/type aliases never touch CLASS_STRUCTS
and go through ALIAS instead.

Fixes #3406.

feat(cli): size WASI browser worker pools from navigator.hardwareConcurrency (#3436)

* feat(cli): size WASI browser worker pools from navigator.hardwareConcurrency

Threaded browser loaders already get a pre-created wasi-threads worker
pool (reuseWorker) and an emnapi async-work pool (asyncWorkPoolSize),
both hardcoded to 4. The constant undersizes both ends of the range:
on an 18-core desktop a hash at p=8 cannot get its helpers, and in a
privacy-fuzzed browser reporting 2 cores the pool oversubscribes.

Both pools are now sized at runtime from
navigator.hardwareConcurrency: logical cores minus one for the main
thread, floored at 2, falling back to 4 when the value is missing or
fuzzed away:

  const __workerPoolSize = Math.max(
    2,
    (globalThis.navigator?.hardwareConcurrency ?? 4) - 1,
  )

Measured with examples/argon2-bench (Chromium, m=64 MiB, t=3): the
dynamic pool covers 7 helpers at p=8 — 11.9 ms vs 68.7 ms at p=1,
a 5.8x parallel speedup that the fixed pool of 4 made impossible.

The pre-created pool is what allows addon Rust code to spawn threads
from inside a blocking call: a browser cannot start a worker until the
blocking thread returns to its event loop, so a thread spawned mid-call
would never boot and the caller would deadlock at its barrier. With a
pre-created pool, spawning is only a message to an already-running
worker. Pool pre-creation is asynchronous, so threaded builds also
initialize asynchronously.

* fix(cli): keep asyncWorkPoolSize at 4; strict reuse pool, verified

Addresses review feedback on #3436, both items verified empirically
before acting:

1. reuseWorker now sets strict: true, as the reviewer suggested, so pool
   exhaustion fails the spawn with a recoverable EAGAIN instead of
   silently allocating a worker that can never boot while the parent is
   blocked. Noted in docs: emnapi ignores strict in Node, so this is a
   browser-only behavior change.

   Strict alone regressed the threaded fill to single-thread speed:
   emnapi's async-work pool draws from the SAME reuse pool, and sizing
   both from hardwareConcurrency left zero slots for addon thread
   spawns (492 "thread pool is exhausted" errors on the first hash).
   asyncWorkPoolSize therefore stays a small constant (4), leaving
   cores-5 slots for Rust thread spawns.

   Verified with examples/argon2-bench (Chromium, m=64 MiB, t=3):
   p=4 19.0 ms, p=8 11.4 ms, p=32 9.3 ms — 13 pooled helpers plus
   graceful EAGAIN fallback for the rest, tags bit-identical.

2. Test assertions strengthened per the nitpick: the threaded test now
   asserts the executable __workerPoolSize expression, strict reuseWorker,
   and asyncWorkPoolSize: 4. Note the review's premise was partially
   off — the generated binding contains "hardwareConcurrency" only in
   the executable expression (the prose comment lives in the template
   source, not the output), which removing the expression proved: the
   original assertion did cover the executable path. The threadless test
   gains the negative __workerPoolSize/hardwareConcurrency/reuseWorker
   and positive asyncWorkPoolSize: 0 checks as suggested.

* fix(cli): reserve async-work workers in the reuse pool; drop strict

Addresses the P1 review finding and the failing "Test node wasi target"
CI job, both verified empirically in Chromium.

The reviewer was right that the reuse pool must include the async-work
reservation: emnapi's async-work pool draws its workers from the same
reuse pool, so on machines reporting 4 or fewer cores the pool (2-3
workers) could not even cover initWorkers(4), failing async-work setup
with EAGAIN — exactly the CI failure ("failed to get new worker" /
WouldBlock in readFileAsync and testWorkers). The reuse pool is now
sized __asyncWorkPoolSize + hardwareConcurrency, so async work always
initializes and addon threads get the full core-derived capacity.

strict is dropped after testing it end-to-end: at exhaustion it breaks
spawn-and-return workloads — the example's own testWorkers (4 workers +
1 joiner thread) panics on EAGAIN — while buying nothing in this
composition. Without strict, the exhausted spawn allocates a fresh
worker that boots as soon as the spawning parent returns to its event
loop, which is how both patterns complete: pooled for speed, fresh for
overflow. Joins inside a blocked call draw from the pre-created pool,
which is the deadlock the pool exists to prevent.

Verified locally with the 4-core CI condition simulated
(__workerPoolSize = 4): all 6 browser tests in examples/napi pass,
including readFileAsync and testWorkers. argon2-bench at p=4/8/32 still
shows 18.8/11.5/114 ms with bit-identical tags.

fix(napi): stop unloading addons with live native code, preserve non-Error rejections, and add the wasm teardown barrier (#3423)

* feat(napi): add Error::from_unknown_without_coercion

JavaScript lets any value be thrown or used to reject a promise, but
`From<Unknown> for Error` assumes an object. It calls
`napi_create_reference` on the value and then `napi_coerce_to_string` on
it, and both are wrong for a value that is not an object:

  * `napi_create_reference` rejects primitives with `napi_invalid_arg`
    below Node-API 10, so the value is lost and replaced by
    `Error { InvalidArg, "Create Error reference failed" }`.
  * `napi_coerce_to_string` runs `toString`/`Symbol.toPrimitive`, that is
    arbitrary user code, while an error is already unwinding.

`from_unknown_without_coercion` does neither. The value is retained
behind a private holder object, which `napi_create_reference` accepts for
every value type, so converting the `Error` back with `ToNapiValue`
reproduces the original value identically. `Error::reason` is filled in
only from data that can be read without running JavaScript: a real
`Error`'s own string `message`, or a string primitive itself. A property
read that throws is swallowed and its exception cleared, so a hostile
accessor cannot poison the environment.

`ErrorRef` grows an `indirect` flag to record that a reference points at
a holder rather than at the value; `referenced_value` unwraps it, so the
indirection never escapes `Error`.

* fix(napi): preserve the value a promise or async generator rejected with

`Promise.reject('boom')` awaited from Rust produced
`Error { InvalidArg, "Create Error reference failed" }`, and
`asyncIterator.throw('boom')` produced the same, because both captured
the value with `From<Unknown> for Error` and `napi_create_reference`
refuses primitives below Node-API 10. Whatever JavaScript actually threw
never reached the addon, and never made it back out to JavaScript either.

Both paths now use `Error::from_unknown_without_coercion`, which retains
the value regardless of its type and derives the reason without running
user code.

`DeferredTrace::into_rejected` needed the matching fix: it reused the
retained value as the rejection whenever that value had a `message`
property, but blanked out `message` and `code` otherwise instead of
falling back to the captured reason. A primitive is not even an object,
so the lookup is now tolerant and the fallback reports what was captured.

* feat(napi): add retain_current_module_for_unload_safety

Node unloads an addon when the environment that loaded it goes away and
no other environment holds it. On Windows that is a `FreeLibrary` which
drops the module's reference count to zero and unmaps the image. Native
code still reachable from a thread that outlives the environment then
points into unmapped memory: the observed symptom is a `0xC0000005`
access violation raised from a Tokio waker vtable, in an addon that was
loaded only inside a worker whose thread then exited.

`retain_current_module_for_unload_safety` takes one extra loader
reference to the image and never releases it, so the addon's code stays
mapped for the rest of the process. Windows uses `GetModuleHandleExW`
with `PIN | FROM_ADDRESS`, declared inline so no new Windows crate is
needed; the dlopen family resolves the image with `dladdr` and bumps its
reference count with `dlopen(RTLD_NOLOAD)`, which is why `libc` is now a
`cfg(unix)` dependency. The reference is taken at most once per process.

It is best effort by design. Targets with no portable loader-pinning
primitive, and failures of the underlying call, leave the image unpinned,
which is exactly the behavior addons had before this existed, so it can
never make things worse than the status quo.

The built-in Tokio runtime is the first caller: `RT` is process-global
and its workers are never joined at environment teardown, so their task
wakers keep vtable pointers into the addon after Node may have unloaded
it. A runtime supplied through `create_custom_tokio_runtime` already owns
threads by the time it is handed over, so that pins immediately rather
than at first use.

* fix(napi): stop aborting the process when a ThreadsafeFunction release fails

`Drop for ThreadsafeFunctionHandle` asserted that
`napi_release_threadsafe_function` returned `napi_ok`. It does not during
an environment teardown: Node closes the threadsafe function first and
reports `napi_closing` to whichever handle drops afterwards. The assert
then panics inside a destructor reached from a Node callback or from a
thread being torn down, unwinds across the FFI boundary, and aborts the
process. Worker exits hit this.

The failure is now handled instead of asserted. Since the release did not
happen, native code that can still reach the threadsafe function may
outlive the environment, so the addon image is retained rather than the
process being torn down.

* fix(napi): release an Error's JS reference only on its owning thread

A `napi_ref` belongs to the env that created it and may only be touched
from that env's JavaScript thread. `ErrorRef` relied on the per-env
custom-GC handle to enforce that, which covers the common case but leaves
two holes:

  * When no handle was captured — a pre-`napi4` build, or a reference
    created before module registration — `ErrorRef::drop` fell through to
    a direct `napi_reference_unref`/`napi_delete_reference` on whatever
    thread the last `Arc` happened to drop on. On native that mutates
    V8's `GlobalHandles` concurrently with the JS thread; the corruption
    surfaces much later as a SIGSEGV inside V8.
  * `Error::referenced_value` likewise read the reference unconditionally
    in that case, and never checked that the `env` it was handed is the
    one the reference was created for.

Record the creating thread in `ErrorRef` and gate both paths on it. A
read from the wrong env or thread reports the reference as absent, so the
caller rebuilds a fresh error from `reason` — the same fallback already
used for an off-thread custom-GC drop. A release from the wrong thread
leaks instead of calling into napi; the leak is bounded, because env
teardown reclaims the reference, while the call is not.

`release_error_reference` also stops deleting a reference whose
`napi_reference_unref` failed: `ref_count` is not meaningful after a
failed call, so the delete was a guess.

* fix(napi): restore JavaScript error identity on wasm targets

On `wasm32-wasip1` and `wasm32-wasip1-threads` a JavaScript error thrown
by user code lost everything but its message on the way to Rust and back.
A `TypeError` carrying a `cause` and custom properties arrived as a bare
`Error { code: 'GenericFailure' }`, because two paths refused to retain
the thrown value on wasm:

  * `retain_value_without_coercion` returned `None`, so
    `Error::from_unknown_without_coercion` — the promise-rejection and
    `AsyncGenerator.throw()` capture path — kept no reference.
  * `call_js_cb` forced `maybe_ref` to `None` for a ThreadsafeFunction
    callback that throws synchronously.

Both were added because releasing the reference from a thread other than
the one that created it crashes the wasi worker with `Cannot read
properties of undefined (reading 'checkGCAccess')`: emnapi resolves
`napi_env` per agent, and a wasi worker has no entry for the main agent's
env (#2975, #3369). The carve-outs predate the per-env custom-GC routing
that now sends such a release back to the owning agent, and were never
revisited afterwards.

They are no longer needed. An off-thread release is routed through the
env's custom-GC threadsafe function — the mechanism `Buffer`,
`TypedArray` and `FunctionRef` already rely on for their own `napi_ref`s
on wasm, with no target carve-out — and the preceding commit makes the
case where no handle was captured leak rather than call into napi.
`Error::referenced_value` refuses to resolve a reference off its owning
env and thread, so an `Error` that travels to a worker still rebuilds a
plain error there instead of dereferencing a foreign env's handle. The
value is retained behind a private holder object, which emnapi accepts
even though it reports Node-API version 8, where `napi_create_reference`
rejects primitives outright.

Retaining the exception in `call_js_cb` also stops reporting its own
failure as the callback's status. That status raises a fatal exception,
so `throw 'oops'` in a ThreadsafeFunction callback — a primitive, which
`napi_create_reference` refuses below Node-API 10 — killed the process
over an error that had already been delivered to the Rust callback. It
survived on wasm only because the carve-out hardcoded `napi_ok`.

The `WASI_TEST` branches that documented the degraded behaviour are gone;
those assertions now match every other target. The generated WASI loaders
pick up `describePromiseRejection`, which they were missing.

* feat(napi): add the napi_prepare_wasm_env_cleanup teardown barrier

Every generated WASI loader — and emnapi's own `disposeNapiModule` — looks
`napi_prepare_wasm_env_cleanup` up on the instantiated module and calls it,
synchronously and on the main thread, as the first step of disposing the
environment. That is the last moment at which the environment is still active
and native code can still call into JavaScript: immediately afterwards
`Env::beginTeardown` flips emnapi's `canCallIntoJs` to `false`, a settle from a
task that is still running can no longer reach its threadsafe function, and the
promise it owned can never settle.

napi never defined the symbol. Native targets get this ordering from Node for
free, because `napi_register_module_v1` registers `thread_cleanup` with
`napi_add_env_cleanup_hook` and Node runs cleanup hooks before it finalizes
threadsafe functions. wasm has no equivalent: the only teardown callback there
is the `exports` finalizer installed with `napi_wrap`, which runs deep inside
the environment teardown, long after JavaScript calls are disabled. So on wasm
the teardown simply happened too late, and a real addon (rolldown) hit it as

    thread '<unnamed>' panicked at crates/napi/src/js_values/deferred.rs:311:
    Call threadsafe function in JsDeferred failed
    RuntimeError: unreachable

Nothing reported the missing barrier, and that is the insidious part.
`napi-build` links the export with `--export-if-defined`, so a binary without
the symbol still links, and every loader guards the call with
`typeof … === 'function'`, so a binary without the symbol still loads and runs.
The link succeeded, the addon loaded, and the drain was silently absent.

The export performs exactly the teardown the `exports` finalizer already
performs — `shutdown_async_runtime()` — only early enough to be useful, so this
adds no new teardown semantics on any target. A registered `AsyncRuntime`
backend's `shutdown` contract makes it a real barrier: it returns only once
every backend-owned thread, task, and blocking closure has quiesced, and tasks
dropped by that shutdown reject their promises through the cancellation
callback, which can still reach JavaScript from here. The built-in Tokio path
keeps its existing best-effort `shutdown_background` semantics: it starts the
drain here instead of after teardown, but does not join Tokio's workers.
Blocking on them would be the wrong trade on wasm, where this runs on the only
thread that can drain the threadsafe-function queue and, in a browser, may not
block at all.

`--export-if-defined` stays: `napi-build` and `napi` are versioned
independently, so a new `napi-build` can still be unified with a `napi` that
predates the symbol, and turning it into a hard `--export` would break that
combination at link time. Detecting an absent barrier is left to a test that
inspects the built artifact instead.

* fix(napi): retain the addon image when a custom async runtime is registered

`retain_current_module_for_unload_safety` had three call sites, and the two
that pin proactively are both behind `cfg(feature = "tokio_rt")`:
`create_runtime` and `create_custom_tokio_runtime`. The third only fires after
a threadsafe-function release has already failed. Nothing on the
`async-runtime` path pinned anything, so an addon that registers a custom
`AsyncRuntime` backend and does not enable `tokio_rt` got no image pinning at
all — its backend threads could outlive the environment and fault after Node
unloaded the addon, which is the exact crash the function was added for.

Pin at publication, inside `try_register`. A published backend is reachable for
the rest of the process: `backend` is a `OnceLock` that is never cleared, and
its trait object's vtable — plus every thread, waker, and destructor the
backend creates in `start` — lives in the addon's image. `shutdown` at a later
environment teardown would call through that vtable after the image could
already have been unmapped. Publication is also the earliest safe point: it
happens exactly once, and it happens before `start` can run, so nothing the
backend creates predates the pin.

`try_register` is the single publication point that both
`register_async_runtime` and `try_register_async_runtime` route through, so
there is no entry point left that can forget. Rejected registrations do not
pin: they are retired through `AsyncRuntime::shutdown` and dropped without ever
becoming reachable.

Like the existing call sites this is `cfg(not(target_family = "wasm"))` —
loader pinning has no meaning for a wasm instance, whose code and environment
share one lifetime.

* fix(napi): settle deferreds with the retained rejection value

A promise may reject, and `AsyncGenerator.throw()` may be called, with any
value. `Error::from_unknown_without_coercion` retains that value, but neither
settle path handed it back:

* with `deferred_trace`, `DeferredTrace::into_rejected` only reused the retained
  value when a `message` property was found on it, so a string, a number or a
  plain object was replaced by the synthetic trace `Error`. For `null` and
  `undefined` it was worse than a replacement: `napi_has_named_property` cannot
  convert them to an object, and the `TypeError` it left pending made the
  following `set_named_property` fail, so the promise never settled at all.
* without `deferred_trace`, `JsError::into_value` gates reuse on `napi_is_error`,
  which rejects every non-`Error` value the same way.

Both now go through the retained value directly — `ToNapiValue for Error` in the
default path — and only fall back to a synthesized error when there is nothing
retained to hand back (an error created in Rust, or converted off its owning
thread). Verified on native in both feature configurations for string, number,
null, undefined, boolean, bigint, symbol, plain object, array, function and
`Error`: every one now settles JavaScript with the identical value.

The tests assert identity rather than the resulting message, which a
freshly synthesized `Error` carrying the same message would also satisfy.

* fix(napi): capture JS errors without ever running a getter

Four defects in the non-coercing capture path, all measured.

1. `Error::reason` claimed to be built "only from data readable without
   running JavaScript" and was not: `message` was read with
   `napi_get_named_property`, an ordinary `[[Get]]`, so a `get message()`
   accessor ran. A fixture whose getter increments a counter reported 1
   invocation.

   Node-API has no descriptor read, but `napi_get_global` and
   `napi_call_function` do exist, so the lookup now goes through
   `Reflect.getOwnPropertyDescriptor`, walking the prototype chain with
   `napi_get_prototype`. A data descriptor contributes its `value`; an
   accessor descriptor stops the walk and is never invoked. The counter
   now reports 0, on the instance and on a subclass prototype alike, and
   a `message` data property up the chain is still found so `new Error()`
   keeps reporting `''` from `Error.prototype.message`.

   Two caveats are documented rather than papered over: a `Proxy` still
   runs its `getOwnPropertyDescriptor`/`getPrototypeOf` traps, and
   `Reflect` is read off the global on every call and is patchable.
   Caching it is deliberately rejected -- it would only move *when* a
   patched `Reflect` is observed, and would need a per-env `napi_ref`
   kept alive across worker teardown.

2. `Error::cause` was hardcoded to `None`, a regression against main on
   the fallback path -- off-thread or a foreign env, exactly where the
   retained value is gone and `JsError::into_value` has to rebuild the
   error from `reason`/`cause`. It is now captured with the same

backend down while the environment can still call into JavaScript, and
the cancelled tasks do reject their `JsDeferred`s from there. But
`napi_call_threadsafe_function` only *appends* to the threadsafe-function
queue. On wasm that queue is dispatched by the host, and @emnapi/core
2.0.0-alpha.3 dispatches a call made on the JavaScript thread from a
macrotask, two coalescing `setImmediate` turns later.

The generated loaders ran the barrier and `Context.destroy()` as two
adjacent synchronous statements:

    __prepareWasmEnvCleanup()
    const result = __emnapiContext.destroy()

`destroy()` runs the threadsafe function's cleanup hook, which drains the
queue with a null env and discards it. So every promise the barrier had
just cancelled was stranded — the exact outcome the barrier exists to
prevent. Measured: 0 of 64 microtask checkpoints ever deliver the
settlement; it takes exactly 2 macrotask turns.

count:

- `napi_wasm_env_cleanup_pending` exports a count of settlements that are
  in the queue but not yet dispatched, maintained by `JsDeferred` around
  `napi_call_threadsafe_function` / `napi_resolve_deferred`. It counts
  only queued settles, never merely-pending promises, so a long-running
  task that shutdown did not cancel cannot make a loader spin.
- The loaders yield real macrotask turns until that count reads zero
  (bounded), then destroy. When nothing is queued the drain returns
  synchronously, so an idle disposal is unchanged.
- The Node `process.on('exit')` fallback cannot yield, so it keeps the
  synchronous teardown and does not get this guarantee.

The behavioral test drove the barrier by hand and awaited the rejection
before `dispose()`, which is what hid this. It now also exercises the
ordinary `dispose()` path end to end in its own process, and the CLI

running the same measurement gives serial 153ms / concurrent 153ms, saved
median 1ms over 15 runs; this branch gives serial 155ms / concurrent 151ms,
saved median 5ms over 25 runs. Every tokio_runtime.rs change here is
cfg(not(target_family = "wasm")). The old fixed 300ms budget passed 122ms
trivially, which is all that was hiding it.

The cause is below napi-rs. Tokio parks a worker on its next timer deadline
through runtime::park::Inner::park_timeout, which is

    #[cfg(all(target_family = "wasm", not(target_feature = "atomics")))]
    { std::thread::sleep(dur) }   // "Wasm without atomics doesn't have threads"

and `target_feature = "atomics"` is never set on wasm32-wasip1-threads --
it is an *unstable* target feature, and rustc does not surface unstable
target features to cfg. `rustc --print cfg --target wasm32-wasip1-threads`
lists bulk-memory and mutable-globals but not atomics, and a crate compiled
with an explicit -Ctarget-feature=+atomics still reports the cfg as false
(rustc warns "unstable feature specified for -Ctarget-feature"). So on the
one wasm target that does have threads, tokio's timer park is an
uninterruptible sleep, even though std's own Condvar::wait_timeout and
thread::park_timeout are fully interruptible there (measured: notify at
20ms interrupts a 200ms wait after 22.2ms).

available_parallelism() is 1 under Node's WASI, so the single worker owns
the time driver, and a task injected from the JavaScript thread is not
polled until the sleep already in flight runs out. Measured first-poll
latency for a task submitted at offset O into a holder sleeping D:
D=200/O=30 -> 152, 133, 116ms; D=400/O=60 -> 314, 286, 323ms -- it tracks
the holder's remaining time, not the injection. With no timer pending the
same injection is polled in 0.11ms, because that path parks on the condvar
instead.

Nothing on napi's own path is at fault. Eight 50ms sleeps joined inside one
task finish in 51ms and eight tokio::spawn'd from within the runtime in
53ms; only the cross-thread wake-up is lost. Patching that single cfg in a
local tokio 1.53.1 checkout takes first-poll latency from ~165ms to 0.2ms
and the same DelayedCounter measurement from serial 155 / concurrent 151 to
serial 184 / concurrent 98 (saved median 91ms). Forcing worker_threads(4)
in create_runtime also recovers it (saved 51-70ms), since the extra workers
park on the multi-thread scheduler's own condvar, which has no wasm
fallback -- but that spawns four Node workers per addon and is a runtime
behavior change, not a test fix.

saving assertion only where the executor can really overlap timers. Both
still fire, verified by breaking DelayedCounter in Rust rather than editing
the test: a turnstile that serialises whole counters trips interleaving on
native *and* on WASI (`aaaaabbbbb`), and a fair FIFO async mutex held across
the sleep trips the saving check on native (serial 154ms, concurrent 153ms,
saved 1ms). Lowering the threshold instead would ship a concurrency
assertion that accepts fully serialised execution.

rejects async work outright ("Built-in Tokio async tasks require a threaded

worker-teardown case it exists for. Placing it in ErrorRef::new covers both
construction sites - the non-coercing capture's private holder and the
From<Unknown> reference - at once. The pin is taken at most once per process;

* fix(napi): resolve Reflect.getOwnPropertyDescriptor once per env at registration

The non-coercing capture reads message/cause through
Reflect.getOwnPropertyDescriptor precisely so that no user code runs while an
error is unwinding - but it resolved Reflect off the global object on every
capture, and that read is an ordinary [[Get]]. globalThis.Reflect is
configurable, so user code can redefine it as an accessor, and the accessor
then runs mid-capture: arbitrary user code, free to reenter the addon or hang,
with side effects that clearing a pending exception cannot undo. Reproduced
empirically: an accessor Reflect fired four times during a single
Error::from_unknown_without_coercion of an error with one cause link.

Resolve the Reflect / getOwnPropertyDescriptor pair once per env, at module
registration, and keep it as own data properties of a private holder behind a
single napi_ref. Capture reads the pair back off the holder - own data
properties of an ordinary object that never escaped to JavaScript, so no
prototype walk and no user code - and never touches the global again.

This inverts the earlier per-call rationale deliberately. That design's
concern was staleness ("caching only changes when a patch is observed"); the
threat model that matters is reentrancy during capture, and the load-time
cache ends it outright - the one unavoidable [[Get]] moves to require() of
the addon, a defined moment, and a post-load patch can no longer inject code
into the capture path at all. The trade is that capture ignores post-load
patches of Reflect instead of observing them late; a data-property Reflect
(the universal case) keeps full behaviour, and an env with no usable cache -
Reflect missing or unusable at registration, or an env that never registered -
degrades to an empty reason/cause, never to a [[Get]] on message. The
reviewer's alternative (omit reason/cause whenever the intrinsic cannot be
obtained without a [[Get]]) is circular on its own: descriptor-reading the
global's Reflect property already requires getOwnPropertyDescriptor.

The per-thread slot leans on the same one-env-per-OS-thread invariant as
CURRENT_CUSTOM_GC_HANDLE. An env cleanup hook (napi3+, native only - wasm-ld
rejects the Rust import of napi_add_env_cleanup_hook against emnapi's archive,
and a wasm slot dies with its instance) deletes the holder reference and
clears the slot at env teardown, so an embedder reusing the thread can never
match a stale entry through a recycled env pointer. Re-registration of the
same env (unload.spec.js) replaces the cache and releases the superseded
reference without re-adding the hook, which Node would abort on.

Guarded by three synchronous-window tests over a new describeCapturedValue
example export: an accessor Reflect must not fire during capture (counter
stays 0) while identity, reason and cause keep full fidelity; a deleted and a
clobbered post-load Reflect keep full fidelity too. Mutation-tested: with the
per-call global lookup restored, all three fail (the accessor fires, and the
reason collapses to "JavaScript Error"). The 11-type identity matrix passes
in both deferred_trace configurations.

* fix(cli): reject the wasm cleanup drain when settlements outlast the turn bound

Both generated drains waited up to 128 macrotask turns for
napi_wasm_env_cleanup_pending to reach zero and then counted reaching the
bound as finished. With the counter still nonzero at the limit that outcome is
indistinguishable from the stranding the drain exists to prevent: disposal
marks the drain complete, destroys the emnapi context, and Context.destroy()'s
cleanup hook discards the still-queued settlement with a null env - the
promise it was for hangs forever with nothing left that could settle it. A
worker-originated settlement whose delivery is delayed past the bound is
enough.

The wait stays bounded, but a still-nonzero counter at the limit now rejects
with ERR_NAPI_WASI_CLEANUP_PENDING instead of setting the drained flag. That
routes the timeout into the machinery the failed-drain paths already have:
dispose() declines to destroy and stays retryable (each retry is one more
bounded wait), the eager rollback retains the context for the registry replay
and process-exit teardown, and the deferred instantiation-failure path
registers the managed beforeExit destroyer. A counter that is somehow stuck
nonzero therefore costs each dispose() attempt a bounded wait and a coded,
retryable rejection - never a stranded promise and never a permanently wedged
process, since the exit-time teardown still reclaims the context. The blind
drain (no pending export) is unchanged: with nothing to consult, the bound is
the contract. Zero at the limit still succeeds.

A genuinely late delivery cannot be produced deterministically - the drain
itself yields the very turns @emnapi/core dispatches on - so the new harness
forces the counter instead: it wraps WebAssembly.Instance.prototype.exports
(a plain per-instance copy; the exports' non-configurable properties bar a
Proxy) and clamps only napi_wasm_env_cleanup_pending to >= 1 while stuck.
Driven against both generated loaders: the first dispose() must reject with
the coded error while the real queue drains unharmed (the in-flight task's
promise settles), and the retry after the clamp lifts must succeed.
Mutation-tested: with the throw reverted to the old "counts as finished"
return, the first dispose() resolves and the harness assertions fail.

The regenerated loaders also pick up the describeCapturedValue export added
by the previous commit. The hand-written threadless-wasi-loader.cjs harness
keeps its minimal bound-counts-as-done drain on purpose: it exists to drive
the barrier from a host's perspective, not to model the retry contract.

constructors (napi_throw, napi_fatal_exception, Env::create_error). On a
settlement path that gate is wrong: an Error that captured an arbitrary JS

back wrong; only a genuine Error survived the gate.

deferred settlement path uses: the retained value comes back verbatim when

other case (an error built on the libuv thread, a capture from a foreign

reference. This is the only napi_create_async_work completion path in the
crate; all three async-work entry points (AsyncTask, Env::spawn,
AbortSignal) settle promises through it, and none of them serves a
non-promise callback variant.
