value types must reject as themselves, mutation-tested against the old
into_value expression (10 failures) in both deferred_trace configurations
and on the wasm32-wasip1-threads lane.

fix(napi): memory safety in PromiseRaw callbacks and AbortSignal conversion (#3458)

* fix(napi): double free and premature free in PromiseRaw then/catch/finally callbacks

The then/catch trampolines freed the boxed Rust callback on every
invocation, and the executed flag was only consulted by the GC finalizer,
so a thenable invoking the callback twice triggered a double free
(CWE-415). finally had neither a flag nor a finalizer: a double
invocation double-freed, and a never-invoked callback leaked.

The boxed callback is now an Option<Cb> owned solely by a napi_wrap
finalizer attached to the callback function itself, so the box lives
exactly as long as the callback is callable. The trampoline borrows the
box and take()s the FnOnce; a second invocation surfaces a JS error
instead of use-after-free. Attaching the finalizer to the callback
function (rather than the object returned by the thenable) also closes
the hole where a thenable that stashes the callback could invoke it
after the returned object was GC'd and the box freed.

Regression tests cover double-invoking thenables (including capturing
closures, since a ZST closure masks the corruption) and a
stash-then-GC scenario.

Refs: GHSA-wrm3-6gmv-vpmw

* fix(napi): type confusion in AbortSignal::from_napi_value and onabort

AbortSignal::from_napi_value called napi_remove_wrap on any JS object
and cast the payload straight to AbortSignalStack with no type check.
A #[napi] class instance wraps a bare *mut T, so passing one as the
signal reinterpreted the victim's fields as a Vec header: stack.0.push
wrote through an attacker-shaped pointer, the victim's own accessors
then read/wrote the fake Vec, and the wrap finalizer eventually freed
an attacker-chosen pointer with the wrong layout. The onabort handler
is an ordinary extractable function value, so stealing it and calling
it with a wrapped receiver reached the same unchecked cast, ending in
an indirect call through a Box<dyn Fn()> (GHSA-qr54-xrr9-7575).

Objects wrapped by AbortSignal::from_napi_value are now stamped with a
dedicated Node object type tag (the same machinery #[napi] classes
use). Conversion rejects objects that are wrapped but do not carry the
tag, and onabort validates its receiver before unwrapping. As with the
class tags, stamping and checking are no-ops on builds without napi8
and on wasm.

Regression tests: a class instance passed as the signal is rejected
and left untouched, a stolen onabort with a foreign receiver throws,
and two tasks sharing one genuine AbortSignal still work.

* test(napi): skip AbortSignal confusion tests on wasm lanes

The type-tag protection is compiled out on wasm targets (type tags are a
no-op there), so the confusion-rejection tests would exercise the
confusion itself and corrupt the test process — observed on the wasi CI
lane as fallout failures in unrelated async task tests.

* fix(napi): protect AbortSignal conversion on all feature levels; close PromiseRaw error-path leaks

Reviewer follow-ups, each verified against the control flow:

- Codex P1: the AbortSignal type-tag guard was a no-op below napi8 and on
  wasm, leaving the default (napi4) feature set exposed. Replace it with a
  process-global registry of live AbortSignalStack allocations: a wrapped
  payload is only cast after its pointer is found in the registry, which
  pure-JS code cannot insert into. Same guarantee on every N-API version
  and on wasm. Verified on both napi4 and napi9 builds.
- Codex P1 (tag-failure rollback): moot under the registry — there is no
  tagging step that can fail after the wrap.
- CodeRabbit Major: the boxed PromiseRaw callback leaked when the
  thenable's then/catch/finally threw during napi_call_function. The
  napi_wrap finalizer now attaches before the call (and the box is
  reclaimed if create_function/wrap itself fails), so every error path
  has an owner.
- CodeRabbit nitpick (valid): the GC test acquired gc from
  globalThis after setFlagsFromString, which never exposes it there, so
  the test silently skipped; pull gc from vm.runInNewContext instead.
- CodeRabbit nitpick (capturing finally fixture): skipped — the existing
  callFinallyOnPromise closure already captures a FunctionRef, so its
  callback box is a real heap allocation.
- The wasm test gate is reverted: the registry protects wasm too, so the
  confusion tests run on the wasi lane again.

* fix(napi): preserve cross-addon AbortSignal sharing via type tags

Codex P2 follow-up: a registry-only discriminator rejects a genuine
AbortSignal that a sibling addon binary (dual-load, or a second addon
built on the same napi version) wrapped first, since each .node has its
own ABORT_SIGNAL_STACKS static. Hybrid recognition: the registry covers
same-binary payloads on every feature level and wasm, and a
version-keyed napi-rs AbortSignal type tag (napi8 native) recognizes
wraps from sibling binaries. Stamping is rolled back (wrap removed, box
reclaimed) if the object turns out to carry a foreign tag.

* fix(napi): never transfer AbortSignal wraps between addons

Codex P1 follow-up: when sibling addon B adopted a wrap installed by
addon A, A's finalizer was detached without running, leaving A's
registry entry permanently stale; a later address reuse could then pass
A's check with a foreign payload. Removes wrap transfer entirely: the
first converter owns the wrap (registry entry + finalizer + tag), and
every later conversion — same or sibling addon — only borrows the
recognized stack to push onto it.

* fix(napi): reject sibling-addon AbortSignal wraps instead of sharing them

Codex P1 follow-up, conflicting with the earlier P2 it replaces: sharing
one AbortSignalStack across addon binaries requires mutating another
binary's Rust Vec (its push may reallocate memory owned by a different
global allocator) and dropping its Rc contents across an unstable ABI.
Cross-addon recognition is therefore removed; a wrap whose payload is
not in this binary's registry is rejected, same or sibling addon alike.
Same-binary sharing is unaffected: the wrap owner keeps the registry
entry and finalizer, later conversions only borrow the stack to push.

* fix(napi): catch panics in closure trampolines instead of aborting

A panic inside a closure registered via `create_function_from_closure`
(or a property getter/setter closure) crossed the `extern "C"`
trampoline, found no landing pad, and aborted the whole Node process:
`rtabort!("failed to initiate panic, error 5")` — the unwind returned
`_URC_END_OF_STACK` because the trampolines sit directly on the FFI
boundary. JS got no exception, and when stderr itself was the failing
pipe (e.g. a full non-blocking test-runner pipe fed by `eprintln!`)
even the panic message was lost, making the crash undebuggable.

- `trampoline`, `trampoline_setter`, `trampoline_getter`: wrap the
  closure call in `catch_unwind` and convert the payload into a JS
  error via `panic_to_error`, flowing through the existing
  `throw_into` path
- `finalize_box_trampoline`: contain finalize-time panics with the
  existing `catch_unwind_safely`, matching the derive-generated
  finalize paths
- behavior is unchanged under `panic = "abort"` builds; this aligns
  the closure paths with the always-on guard on async functions and
  the `#[napi(catch_unwind)]` opt-in on sync functions

Add `create_panicking_closure_function` plus a spec asserting the
panic surfaces as a catchable JS error (previously: SIGABRT).

* fix(napi): cover N-API conversions and payload drops in the closure panic guard

Review follow-up to the closure trampoline catch_unwind: two escape
hatches remained where a panic could still cross the extern "C"
boundary and abort the process instead of surfacing as a JS error.

- the guards wrapped only the closure call; the surrounding
  ToNapiValue/FromNapiValue conversions are public extension points,
  so a panic in `Return::to_napi_value`, `R::to_napi_value`,
  `V::from_napi_value`, or the `This` conversion still unwound through
  the trampolines. The guard now encloses the complete
  callback-plus-conversion path in all three trampolines.
- `panic_to_error` consumes the panic payload by value, so a payload
  whose `Drop` impl panics blows up after `catch_unwind` has already
  returned — outside any guard. Replaced it at the three call sites
  with `panic_payload_to_error`, which extracts the message first and
  then leaks the payload (`mem::forget`, mirroring
  `catch_unwind_safely`), falling back to `Status::GenericFailure`.
  The helper itself cannot panic.

Also drop `panic_to_error` from the env.rs imports: its only users are
`#[cfg(feature = "napi5")]`, which previously produced an unused-import
warning on builds without napi5.

* fix(napi): drop panic payloads under containment in panic_payload_to_error

The panic payload conversion helper retained every caught payload, so a
closure that panics on each call grew native memory without bound. Drop
the payload through `catch_unwind_safely` instead: it contains a
panicking `Drop` impl and leaks only the nested panic payload, keeping
the second panic from crossing the extern "C" trampoline.

fix: CurrentThread waker-stack deadlocks and threadless-wasm Buffer detachment (#3489)

* fix(async-runtime): never drop a rejected CurrentThread runnable inline on the waker's thread

Cancelling queued work after a terminal host-dispatch failure drops each
runnable with no executor lock held, but the drop itself can run inside a
foreign lock: dropping task A's runnable closes A and notifies its awaiter,
and when that awaiter is a `futures::Shared` its notifier wakes every
registered waker while holding its own `wakers` mutex. If one of those
wakers belongs to a parked, unscheduled task B, `async-task` schedules B,
`CurrentThreadExecutor::schedule` sees `cancelling_failed_dispatch` and
dropped B's runnable right there. B's future owns a clone of the same
`Shared`, whose destructor re-locks `wakers` on the same thread, so the
thread hangs forever. rolldown hit exactly this on `ROLLDOWN_RUNTIME=single`
when a `worker_threads` Worker running watch mode was terminated with the
debounce timer armed: the env cleanup hook unregisters the only task driver,
the coordinator runnable is cancelled, and the Worker never leaves
`node::FreeEnvironment`.

`schedule` now defers such runnables into `CurrentThreadQueue::rejected`
(guarded by the existing queue mutex) instead of dropping them, and the
cancellation sweep drains that list on its own stack after releasing every
lock, looping because each drop can reject more. The executor is reopened
while holding the queue lock, which `schedule` also holds when it consults
the flag, so nothing can land in the list after the final drain.
`begin_shutdown` takes the list too, in case a sweep races shutdown. The
`queue.closed` reject branch keeps dropping inline: `close_and_abort` has
already scheduled every registered task by then, and deferring there would
hold `GenerationWorkGuard`s that `wait_until_idle` waits on.

The new unit test reproduces the shape with a real `Shared` and fails with a
5-second timeout instead of hanging on the unfixed code.

* fix(async-runtime): defer closed-queue CurrentThread rejections to the shutdown side

The previous commit left the `queue.closed` reject branch dropping the
runnable inline, arguing `close_and_abort` had already scheduled every
registered task. That misses a wake that is already in flight when
shutdown starts: `async-task` sets SCHEDULED before it invokes the
schedule closure, so a waker thread can be descheduled between that CAS
and the executor's queue lock. The abort `close_and_abort` issues for the
same task then coalesces with the in-flight wake and returns, and
`begin_shutdown` closes the queue without waiting for the closure to
land. When the closure resumes it is rejected by the closed queue and,
if the waker was `futures::Shared`'s notifier (still holding `wakers`),
dropping the future inline re-locks `wakers` from its `Shared` clone and
hangs; the task's `GenerationWorkGuard` never retires, so
`wait_until_idle` hangs with it.

`schedule` now parks closed-queue rejections in `queue.rejected` too and
wakes the generation's idle waiter. The executor is attached to its
`GenerationWork` by the backend, and `RuntimeBackend::wait_until_idle`
retires the parked runnables on its own stack, on every iteration, until
the generation is idle; `notify_idle_waiters` publishes under the state
lock so the check cannot miss a late arrival. `wait_until_scheduler_idle`
and the executor's destructor drain the list for executors that are torn
down without a backend, so no runnable (and no guard) can outlive the
executor. The regression test pauses B's schedule closure inside the
Shared notifier while `begin_shutdown` runs, and timed out on the
previous commit.

* fix(async-runtime): never run the CurrentThread cancellation sweep on a waker's stack

The two previous commits stopped `schedule` from dropping a rejected
runnable inline, but the terminal-failure sweep itself could still run on
the waker's stack. `schedule` publishes a host dispatch whenever it queues
work, and if the host fails that delivery before `dispatch` returns (a
threadsafe function that is closing does exactly this while an env tears
down) and fails the one replacement the same way, `publish_host_dispatch`
enters the terminal transition and ran
`cancel_work_after_host_dispatch_failure_claimed` right there. When the
waker was `futures::Shared`'s notifier, still holding `wakers`, dropping a
queued task that owns a clone of that `Shared` re-locked `wakers` on the
same thread and hung; deferring into `queue.rejected` did not help because
the sweep's own drain loop dropped the deferred runnable on that stack too.

Every waker reaches the executor through `schedule`, so a thread-local
depth (`CurrentThreadScheduleScope`) now marks stacks that may belong to a
waker. A terminal transition reached at nonzero depth only publishes the
closed state: `cancelling_failed_dispatch` stays set (schedules keep
deferring, no dispatch is published) and the sweep is parked in
`failed_dispatch_sweep_pending`. Clean stacks reclaim it: every host entry
point (`complete_current_thread_task_delivery`, which also covers a driver
unregistration that carries no failure, `cancel_host_dispatch`,
`request_drain_if_queued` for a re-registering host) when not inside
`schedule`, and unconditionally `begin_shutdown`, the generation's idle wait
(which now also treats a parked sweep as deferred work, so the queued
`GenerationWorkGuard`s cannot outlive `wait_until_idle`),
`wait_until_scheduler_idle` and the executor's destructor. Reclaiming is a
single compare-exchange, so a sweep runs at most once and reopens the
executor exactly as before. Runnables are `Send`, but running the sweep on
a helper thread was rejected: the crate has no such worker, threadless
builds have no second thread, and host-affine futures must keep being
destroyed on host or shutdown threads.

The new unit test ports the reviewer's reproduction with a driver that
fails accepted deliveries synchronously and timed out on the previous
commit.

* fix(async-runtime): reopen the CurrentThread executor at once after a waker-stack terminal failure

The previous commit parked the terminal-failure cancellation sweep when the
transition was reached on a waker's stack and left the executor closed
(`cancelling_failed_dispatch` set) until a clean stack reclaimed the sweep.
That has no continuation of its own: with the driver still registered and
healthy again, every later `schedule` took the closed branch, was deferred
into `queue.rejected` and published no host delivery, so neither the
pre-failure work nor anything submitted afterwards ever ran. Only an
unprompted external entry (`request_current_thread_task_drain`, an
unregistration, shutdown) could reopen it; the previous regression test
supplied exactly such a drain and masked the stall.

The transition now moves instead of parking. Under the queue lock it moves
the queued runnables (with their `queued_runnables` debit) and the queued
blocking jobs into `queue.rejected` / `queue.rejected_blocking`, and then:

  * on a clean stack it drops that work right there, with the executor
    still closed so the tasks those drops wake are rejected and cancelled
    with it, and reopens under the queue lock once nothing remains. This
    is the ordering terminal cancellation always had; the timer-relay and
    Shared-awaiter tests depend on it (queued work and everything it wakes
    settle at once, no later host work is published);
  * on a waker's stack it drops nothing and reopens immediately. The next
    submission takes the ordinary path and publishes its own delivery, and
    the moved work is cancelled by `retire_rejected_work` on the next clean
    stack: the host turn that services that delivery
    (`drive_admitted_host_turn`), any other host entry point (delivery
    completion, unregistration, `cancel_host_dispatch`,
    `request_drain_if_queued`), or the shutdown side (`begin_shutdown`, the
    generation's idle wait, `wait_until_scheduler_idle`, the destructor).

The moved runnables keep their `GenerationWorkGuard`s, so the transition
notifies idle waiters and the idle wait retires rejected work exactly as it
did for closed-queue rejections. The drain loops terminate: each drop closes
one task for good, and a nested transition needs two more host-failed
deliveries of its own.

Deleted: `failed_dispatch_sweep_pending`, `run_pending_failed_dispatch_sweep`
and its `_off_waker_stack` twin, `CurrentThreadDispatchCancellationGuard::
defer`, `has_deferred_shutdown_work` / `retire_deferred_shutdown_work`, and
the `_claimed` split of the transition. `has_rejected_runnables` /
`retire_rejected_runnables` became `has_rejected_work` /
`retire_rejected_work`, which also cover the rejected blocking jobs. The
thread-local schedule depth stays: it is what tells the two branches apart
and gates the host-entry drains.

Tests: a fourth regression test ports the reviewer's reproduction (driver
stays registered, turns healthy, no drain request); it failed on the
previous commit with three deliveries instead of four. The third test now
observes the cancellation through a host turn instead of the drain request.

* docs(async-runtime): state the CurrentThreadTaskDriver::dispatch blocking contract

`dispatch` is called from `schedule`, which may be a waker's stack while the
waker's producer holds a lock (`futures::Shared` wakes under `wakers`). A
terminal delivery failure cancels the rejected work on the stack of the
thread that failed it, and a rejected future's destructor may re-lock that
same mutex. A driver whose `dispatch` blocks its caller on the thread that
later fails the delivery (spawn a helper that calls
`fail_current_thread_task_delivery`, then join it) therefore deadlocks, on
this branch and on every earlier release alike.

Document the contract on the trait method: return promptly, never wait on
another thread, in particular not on the one that will acknowledge or fail
the delivery. Failing synchronously from inside `dispatch` on the calling
thread is handled (the executor treats that stack as a possible waker's and
defers the cancellation), and so is failing or acknowledging later from any
thread. The Node-API driver in `adapter.rs` already satisfies this: one
nonblocking threadsafe-function call, `false` at once on `napi_closing`.

* test(async-runtime): pin MultiThread closed-queue rejection does not drop inline

Audit of every place the MultiThread executor drops a `Runnable` or a
blocking job outside of running it, prompted by the PR note that
`MultiThreadExecutor::schedule` "still has a closed-queue inline drop":

  * `MultiThreadExecutor::schedule` has no closed-queue branch for runnables
    at all. Every runnable goes to the worker's LIFO slot or to the injector
    (`push_to_queue_and_wake`), stop published or not. The only inline drop
    on the submission side is `schedule_blocking_result`'s closed
    `blocking_queue` branch, which destroys a blocking closure and its
    result sender on the `spawn_blocking` caller's stack; the runtime's own
    wakers never reach it (`Waker::wake` -> `WeakRuntimeExecutor::schedule`
    -> `MultiThreadExecutor::schedule`), and dropping the sender only wakes
    the awaiting task, which is a push, not a drop.
  * A runnable that lands after `begin_shutdown` is cancelled when a drainer
    (or a cooperative `block_on` driver) claims it under the published stop:
    `claim_runnable` / `claim_fifo_runnable` -> `RunnableClaim::Cancel` ->
    `cancel_runnable`, on that claimer's own stack, never the waker's.
  * `begin_shutdown` drops the queued blocking jobs on the shutdown caller's
    stack; shutdown from runtime work is rejected before that.
  * The executor's implicit `Drop` (injector, blocking queue) runs after the
    generation is idle, i.e. after every task future is gone, so no runnable
    can still be queued and no waker can still reach `schedule`.

So the CurrentThread bug shape (a wake already SCHEDULED but not yet at the
queue when shutdown closes it, resumed under `futures::Shared`'s `wakers`
lock, and the rejected future re-locking it from its destructor) has no
MultiThread counterpart: the late runnable is accepted and cancelled
elsewhere. This test transposes the CurrentThread regression test one to
one and passes on the current tree. Two throwaway runs back the pin: with a
CT-style inline drop added to `schedule` behind `stop.is_stopping()` the
test times out after 5 s, and with `cancel_runnable` instrumented the real
cancellation is logged on pool worker `mt-inline-drop-0`
(`ON_POOL_WORKER` set), not on the waker thread.

No production code changes.

* fix(napi): copy Buffers on threadless wasm so memory growth cannot detach them

`Test custom async runtime on wasm32-wasip1` has been red on every branch
since 2026-09-07: `examples/napi/wasi-public-surface/test.mjs` asserted
`'' !== 'Hello world'` for a `Buffer` the addon had just returned.

Root cause is an asymmetry inside emnapi. `napi_create_external_arraybuffer`
copies the bytes into a JS-owned `ArrayBuffer`, but
`napi_create_external_buffer` is implemented as a *view* over wasm linear
memory. A threadless wasm target has a non-shared memory, and the spec says
every `memory.grow` on a non-shared memory detaches the previous
`ArrayBuffer`. So any `Buffer` that JS is still holding across an allocation
that grows the heap silently becomes a zero-length view: `.length` reads 0
and `.toString()` reads `''`, with no error anywhere. Threaded wasm targets
use a shared memory whose old views stay valid, so they are unaffected.

Whether a grow lands between the call that returned the `Buffer` and the read
is a layout lottery: it depends on where `__heap_base` falls relative to a
64 KiB page boundary. The `encoding_rs` 0.8.40 bump added 16 bytes of
`.rodata`, which shifted `__heap_base` just enough that the first heap
allocation now crosses a page and grows the memory. That is a layout shift,
not an `encoding_rs` defect - the bug was latent in every earlier build and
the bump only exposed it.

The fix adds a `create_external_buffer` wrapper in
`crates/napi/src/bindgen_runtime/js_values/buffer.rs`. Under
`cfg(all(target_family = "wasm", not(target_feature = "atomics")))` it
returns `napi_no_external_buffers_allowed` instead of calling into emnapi, so
the three call sites - `BufferSlice::from_data`, `BufferSlice::from_external`
and `Buffer::to_napi_value` - take the `napi_create_buffer_copy` fallback
they already carry for Electron. The result is a JS-owned, growth-immune
`Buffer`. No new code path is introduced; each fallback still reclaims its
leaked `Box` exactly once, and the `BUFFER_DATA` double-use registry is
`not(target_family = "wasm")` so it is untouched. Typed arrays and
`ArrayBuffer` need no change because their emnapi entry point already copies.

The two `crates/napi/src/env.rs` sites are deliberately left alone: their
fallback reuses the `result_data` pointer returned by
`napi_create_buffer_copy`, which on emnapi points at a runtime-owned mirror
rather than at the caller's allocation, so routing them through the same
wrapper would hand out a pointer with the wrong ownership.

`examples/napi` gains a `wasmMemorySizeBytes()` export. The workerd growth
fixture used to measure linear memory as `getBuffer().buffer.byteLength`;
now that a threadless `Buffer` is a copy, that probe no longer mirrors the
wasm memory, so it reads `core::arch::wasm32::memory_size(0)` through the
addon instead.

Three regression tests hold a `Buffer` across a deliberate `memory.grow` and
assert it still reads `'Hello world'`: the node spec
`__tests__/wasi-buffer-public-api.spec.ts`, the browser fixture
`wasi-public-surface/browser/test.mjs`, and the workerd fixture
`wasi-public-surface/workerd/worker.mjs`. All three fail on the unfixed tree
and pass with the fix.

* fix(async-runtime): give an ordinary CurrentThread spawn its own continuation

`async-task` runs one scheduler callback for two different things: a wake,
which any `Waker` can raise from any stack, and the very first schedule of a
freshly submitted task, which `spawn` makes on its caller's own stack. The
previous commit entered `CURRENT_THREAD_SCHEDULE_DEPTH` around all of
`schedule`, so it could not tell them apart and treated both as a waker's
stack.

The interleaving that leaves: `spawn` queues the runnable and publishes a host
dispatch; the host accepts the callback and fails the delivery before
`dispatch` returns (a threadsafe function that is closing does exactly this),
and fails the one replacement the same way. `publish_host_dispatch` reaches the
terminal transition still inside that submission's `schedule` frame, sees a
nonzero depth, moves the runnable into `queue.rejected`, reopens and returns.
No host turn ever ran, `complete_current_thread_task_delivery` has already
been called, and nothing else reaches `retire_rejected_work`: without a later
submission, an explicit drain, an unregistration or shutdown, the returned
`JoinHandle` stays pending forever and its `GenerationWorkGuard` stays active.
Reproduced through the public API with a plain `spawn` from the main thread,
no waker and no `futures::Shared` anywhere: dispatches=2,
queued_runnables=0, handle pending, future destructor never run.

The depth counter now marks only the frames a waker could have entered.
`schedule` (the `async-task` callback, reachable from any `Waker::wake`) keeps
entering the scope; `schedule_submission`, called only by
`RuntimeBackend::schedule_submission` for a task's first schedule, does not.
A submission's terminal failure therefore cancels its rejected work right
there -- the only continuation it has -- while a genuine wake still defers,
because the waker's producer may hold a mutex the destructors re-lock
(`futures::Shared` wakes under its `wakers` lock). The wake-stack branch is
untouched, so the executor still reopens at once instead of stalling a
healthy, still-registered driver.

Nesting stays conservative: a submission made from inside a wake frame does
not clear the outer scope, so the depth stays nonzero and the transition
still defers.

* fix(napi): point BufferSlice at the buffer data instead of the napi_value

`BufferSlice`'s three constructors built `inner` from `buf`, the `napi_value`
out-param, instead of from the buffer's data pointer. Since `raw_value` got the
same variable, `inner.as_ptr() == raw_value` on every path, so `Deref`,
`DerefMut`, `AsRef` and `AsMut` addressed the handle, not the bytes: on native
Node the V8 handle slot (reads return garbage), on wasm32-wasip1 the emnapi
handle id, i.e. linear-memory address 9.

This affects every constructor on every platform - native, Electron, threaded
and threadless wasm alike - not only the threadless-wasm copy fallback added
earlier on this branch. `FromNapiValue` was already correct, because it reads
through `napi_get_buffer_info`; the constructors simply disagreed with the
reader. `Buffer::to_napi_value`'s fallback only produces a `napi_value` and
builds no slice, so it was never affected.

Pointer now used per path:

  from_data     external ok  -> the `Vec`'s `inner_ptr`
                copy fallback -> `napi_get_buffer_info` on the new buffer
  from_external external ok  -> the caller's `data`
                copy fallback -> `napi_get_buffer_info` on the new buffer
  copy_from                  -> `napi_get_buffer_info` on the new buffer

The copy paths deliberately do not use `napi_create_buffer_copy`'s
`result_data` out-param, even though `env.rs` can. Under emnapi that pointer is
wrong: `napi_create_buffer_copy` allocates the copy as a JS-owned `ArrayBuffer`,
writes a lazily-mirrored wasm address into `result_data`, and only afterwards
copies the bytes into the `ArrayBuffer` - so `result_data` points at a still
zero-filled mirror. `napi_get_buffer_info` is the call that refreshes that
mirror, which makes it the only pointer that is correct on every target. It is

* fix(async-runtime): give a CurrentThread wake's terminal failure its own continuation

`6d452174` gave an ordinary submission a continuation; a genuine wake still
had none. The interleaving:

  * a task is delivered, driven and parks on a wakeable (`futures::Shared`, a
    oneshot, a timer);
  * its waker fires. `schedule` enters `CurrentThreadScheduleScope`, queues the
    runnable and publishes a host dispatch;
  * the host fails that delivery before `dispatch` returns (a closing
    threadsafe function, or any SPI host taking the synchronous-failure option
    `CurrentThreadTaskDriver::dispatch` documents), and fails the one
    replacement the same way;
  * `publish_host_dispatch` reaches the terminal transition at nonzero depth.
    It moves the runnable into `queue.rejected`, reopens, notifies generation
    idle waiters and returns -- correctly dropping nothing on a stack that may
    be under a foreign lock.

What it left behind was nothing at all. The transition consumed the executor's
one outstanding host request (`dispatch_pending` is 0) and emptied the queue,
so `has_serviceable_work` is false and neither `request_drain_if_work_remains`
nor a later wake of an already-parked task publishes again. During normal
operation there is no generation idle waiter either. The moved runnable kept
its `JoinHandle` and its `GenerationWorkGuard` until some unrelated entry
happened to arrive: a later submission, a drain request, an unregistration or
shutdown. Reproduced through the public API with a CurrentThread driver, a
task parked on a `futures::channel::oneshot` and no activity after the wake:
dispatches during the wake = 2, queued_runnables = 0, handle pending, the
future's destructor never run.

The waker-stack branch now publishes one fresh host dispatch for itself after
it reopens. A host turn is precisely the clean stack that retires the moved
work -- `drive_admitted_host_turn` calls `retire_rejected_work_off_waker_stack`
before it polls anything -- and the executor is already open, so this takes the
ordinary publication path and cannot starve a healthy registered driver. A
thread-local one-shot (`CURRENT_THREAD_RETIRING_REJECTED_WORK`) bounds it: that
publication calls the driver again, so a runnable another thread queues
meanwhile can drive a nested terminal transition on this same stack, and
without the one-shot a producer could recurse the stack without bound. It is
thread-local, not per-executor, because the bound it enforces is a stack bound
and a transition on another thread must keep its own continuation.

Nothing is destroyed on the waker's stack: this adds no `retire_rejected_work`
call. A nested transition inside the new publication still sees the outer
`CurrentThreadScheduleScope` and takes the waker branch, and the
`complete_current_thread_task_delivery` the driver runs there reaches only
`retire_rejected_work_off_waker_stack`, which returns at nonzero depth.

Rejected alternatives:

  * Retiring at the end of the OUTERMOST `schedule` frame, when the depth
    counter returns to zero. The stated grounds -- async-task's wake callback
    returns to its caller before the caller releases its lock -- is exactly why
    this does not work: `futures::Shared` calls `wake` on each awaiter from
    inside its notify loop while holding `wakers`, so depth 0 at scope exit is
    still under that mutex, and a rejected future owning a `Shared` clone
    re-locks it on drop. That is the deadlock `8565a599` and `09905d45` fixed.
  * Handing the rejected work (and `rejected_blocking`) to another thread.
    Runnables are `Send`, but threadless wasm has no second thread and
    host-affine futures must be destroyed on a host or shutdown thread. Already
    rejected in `09905d45` for the same reasons.

When the host never recovers, the new publication fails or reports no live
driver, and that is terminal by construction: the queue is empty, so
`begin_host_dispatch_failure_transition_locked` reserves no replacement and no
further publication follows. The work then waits for the next host that
registers (`request_drain_if_queued` retires before it publishes) or for
shutdown. That is the honest limit of a host-driven executor: with no host
there is no stack on which user futures may be destroyed.

Tests: a fifth regression test parks B on a `futures::Shared`, loses exactly
the wake's publication and its one replacement, and then lets the host service
only the delivery the transition published for itself -- no later submission,
no drain request, no unregistration, no shutdown. It saw three deliveries
instead of four on the previous commit and B never settled. The two existing
waker-stack tests now count that extra self-published delivery.

* fix(async-runtime): hand a nested CurrentThread retirement request back to its owner

`fc4d8e3b` gave a waker-stack terminal failure a continuation: it publishes
one fresh host dispatch for itself, and the host turn that services it is the
clean stack on which `retire_rejected_work` cancels the moved work. That
publication calls the host driver again, so a thread-local one-shot
(`CURRENT_THREAD_RETIRING_REJECTED_WORK`) bounds it -- and the one-shot
DISCARDED a nested request instead of handing it back:

  thread W (waker)                      | thread T (producer)
  --------------------------------------+------------------------------------
  Shared notifier wakes B -> schedule   |
  publish D1 ................. fails    |
  publish D2 (replacement) ... fails    |
  terminal #1: B -> queue.rejected,     |
    reopen (drop nothing here)          |
  retirement scope ENTER, publish D3 ---+--> schedule(C) -> queue.runnables
                                        |    request_drain -> Coalesced (D3)
  D3 fails, has_serviceable_work(C)     |
  publish D4 (replacement) ... fails    |
  terminal #2: C -> queue.rejected,     |
    reopen                              |
  retirement scope already ACTIVE       |
    -> return, publishing NOTHING       |

Four deliveries during the wake, all lost, no host turn ran, `dispatch_pending`
back to 0 and `has_serviceable_work` false -- so nothing published again. Both
B's and C's runnables stayed in `queue.rejected` with their `JoinHandle`s
pending, their futures never destroyed and their `GenerationWorkGuard`s live,
even though the host was healthy for its very next delivery. Measured on
`fc4d8e3b`: dispatches during the wake = 4, terminal transitions = 2 (both on
the waker's stack), discarded retirement requests = 1, host turns = 0,
`queued_runnables` = 0, neither handle settled, neither future dropped.

The nested transition now records its request in
`CURRENT_THREAD_REJECTED_WORK_RETIREMENT_REQUESTED` and the frame that owns the
publication loops: it publishes, and after its own publication has fully
unwound it takes the flag and publishes again while rejected work remains.
Nothing is destroyed on the waker's stack -- this adds no `retire_rejected_work`
call, and the continuation is still a published host dispatch retired later at
depth 0 by `drive_admitted_host_turn`.

Termination. Each turn makes exactly one publication. Another turn happens only
if a nested terminal transition ran inside it, which needs the host to fail two
more deliveries AND at least one runnable or blocking job newly queued in that
window; with an empty queue the first failure reserves no replacement, so no
transition and no request follow. Rejected work is never re-scheduled while it
waits (`async-task` keeps such a task SCHEDULED because its runnable still
exists, so its wakers are no-ops), so every turn consumes one distinct live task
or blocking job and none can supply a second. The first publication the host
accepts ends the loop, because an accepted delivery fails nothing. A permanently
dead host therefore exits after one turn, with the work waiting for the next
registering host or for shutdown -- the limit already documented on this branch:
with no host there is no stack on which user futures may be destroyed. The stack
does not grow either way: the nested call returns at once and the retry is a
loop in the owner frame, so at most two transition frames are live.

Design. The flag stays thread-local, next to the one-shot it repairs, because
the bound being enforced is a STACK bound: only a nested call on this same stack
would recurse. A terminal transition on another thread finds the one-shot clear
and keeps publishing its own continuation, which is correct -- its stack is its
own. Rejected: moving the pending-request flag onto the executor. It would have
turned that self-contained cross-thread continuation into a hand-off to a frame
on another thread, which needs a release-then-recheck dance to close the
set-vs-clear window and can publish a spurious extra delivery when both threads
service the same flag -- two atomics and a lost-request proof, for a case that
was not broken. It also would not have covered what a plain executor flag is
sometimes credited with: a nested transition for a DIFFERENT executor on this
stack still finds the thread-local one-shot held and records nothing anyone
services, because a per-executor flag has no owner frame to drain it. Covering
that needs per-(thread, executor) keying; I found no path to it in this crate
(it takes two CurrentThread executors whose host dispatch callbacks interleave
on one stack) and left it out rather than widen this fix.

Tests: a sixth regression test drives exactly the interleaving above -- B parks
on a `futures::Shared`, a producer thread queues C from inside the retirement
turn's publication through a driver hook, the host loses all four deliveries and
is healthy from the fifth -- and then services only that fifth delivery. It saw
five deliveries instead of six on the previous commit and neither B nor C ever
settled.

rejected work is never re-scheduled while it waits -- is true, and bounds the

  Shared notifier wakes B -> schedule   |
  publish D1 ---------------------------+--> schedule(C1) -> queue.runnables
  host fails D1 synchronously           |    request_drain -> Coalesced (D1)
  publish D2 (replacement) -------------+--> schedule(C2)
  host fails D2 synchronously           |

    reopen (drop nothing here)          |
  retirement turn 1: publish D3 --------+--> schedule(C3)
  host fails D3, sees C3 serviceable    |

  host fails D4                         |
  terminal #2 -> request handed back    |
  retirement turn 2: publish D5 --------+--> ... and so on, forever

flight, so it never blocks and never runs dry. Measured on `e2a8ed9c` with a

notify loop, so its `wakers` mutex is held for the whole time; any producer
lock beneath the waker is held with it. This is latency and lock hold, not a
deadlock: reachable only for an SPI host that fails deliveries synchronously
from inside `dispatch`, since the built-in Node-API host returns `false` when
the environment is closing (adapter.rs:654-676) and only ever fails a delivery
from the threadsafe-function callback on the JS thread (adapter.rs:455-473) --

which `e2a8ed9c`'s test pins); 8 leaves slack for a short burst of genuinely

producer's mutex, which is the thing being held; parking the leftover request

`queue.rejected` still holding the wake's runnable. Measured before this commit,
with a host that refuses the wake's publication, its one replacement and all

inside `dispatch`: 11 deliveries during the wake, `dispatch_pending` 0,

driver registered and healthy for its very next one.

An offer the host ACCEPTED but could not act on leaves exactly the state a
REFUSED one leaves, so it is owed exactly the same thing, and the condition this
branch already reads off the executor says so:
`needs_rejected_work_retirement_dispatch` -- work parked and no dispatch
outstanding. So `publish_final_rejected_work_retirement` now reports whether the

followed by one ordinary publication. The executor is open again by then, which
is what `5857092f` reopened it for, so this takes the ordinary path. A refused
offer still leaves nothing behind, so no test whose host refuses everything
changes its delivery count.

terminal transition nested inside it finds `CURRENT_THREAD_RETIRING_REJECTED_WORK`
held by this frame and publishes nothing, so at most its own one reserved
replacement follows it. Measured with the host refusing every delivery from the
inline service onwards: exactly 12 deliveries during the wake, and the wake
returned.

Nothing is destroyed on any waker-reachable stack: this adds no
`retire_rejected_work` call. The producer bound is untouched -- the budget still
caps the turns a producer can inflate, and this publication is as uninflatable as
the offer it follows, because it is made once.

End state. A host that consumes this publication on the waker's stack too has
never left that stack, and that is the limit this branch already documents: with
no host turn on a clean stack there is nowhere to destroy a user future, and the
work waits for the next host that registers or for shutdown.

fix(macro): recognize fully-qualified napi::Env as the special Env parameter (#3486)

* fix(macro): recognize fully-qualified napi::Env as the special Env parameter

The #[napi] macro special-cases a function parameter of type `Env` so it
receives the callback's `Env` directly instead of going through the normal
`FromNapiValue` argument conversion. This check compared the parameter's
entire token stream against the literal string "Env", which only matches
the bare identifier. Writing the type as a qualified path such as
`napi::Env` or `napi::env::Env` produces a different token stream (e.g.
"napi :: Env"), so the special case silently failed to trigger and the
argument fell through to normal conversion, causing a confusing
"the trait bound `Env: NapiValue` is not satisfied" compile error.

Fix both places in the backend crate that performed this whole-token-stream
comparison (codegen and typegen) to instead match on the resolved type's
last path segment ident, which is the idiom already used elsewhere in the
same files for other special-cased parameter types (`Reference`, `This`,
etc.) and in the parser crate for `Env`/`Object` detection in
`module_exports`. This makes the check independent of how many path
segments precede `Env`, so bare `Env`, `napi::Env`, and `napi::env::Env`
are all recognized consistently.

Added a regression test in examples/napi-cargo-test asserting that a
#[napi] function taking `napi::Env` (fully qualified) compiles.

Fixes #1597

* Guard Env detection against qualified-self paths

The last-path-segment match added for #1597 only checked the final
ident, so a qualified-self path like <T as Trait>::Env whose
associated type happens to be named Env would also match and get
silently treated as napi's special environment parameter instead of
being extracted normally via FromNapiValue.

Require qself.is_none() alongside the ident check in both the
codegen and typegen Env-detection sites, matching CodeRabbit's review
on the open PR. Added a regression test using a qualified-self
associated type named Env that only compiles if it is NOT special-cased.

* fix(macro): guard borrowed Env detection against qualified-self paths

The qself guard for by-value Env parameters was missing from the
borrowed-parameter branch of codegen, so `&<T as Trait>::Env` was still
injected as the napi environment while typegen (already guarded) kept it
as a regular argument — the generated .d.ts disagreed with runtime
argument consumption.

Add the same qself: None requirement to the borrowed check and regression
coverage for a borrowed qualified-self associated type named Env.

fix(napi): point from_external slices at the engine-owned copy after finalize reclaims the source (#3503)

* fix(napi): point from_external slices at the engine-owned copy after finalize reclaims the source

On the napi_no_external_buffers_allowed fallback (Electron, V8-sandbox
builds), ArrayBuffer::from_external, TypedArraySlice::from_external,
Uint8ClampedSlice::from_external and the compat-mode
Env::create_arraybuffer_with_borrowed_data copied the caller's bytes
into an engine-owned ArrayBuffer, ran the caller's finalize callback -
which by contract reclaims the source allocation - and then built the
returned Rust slice from the just-freed source pointer. Any Rust-side
read or write through the slice was a use-after-free; the freed
allocation is typically reused immediately, so reads return
attacker-influenced bytes and writes corrupt live allocations.

The slices now point at the engine-owned copy on the fallback path, the
same construction BufferSlice's constructors adopted in bbebbb4b for
GHSA-3hv5-cch8-c72w.

Verified on the repo's Electron lane (sandboxed V8 forces the
fallback): with the fix reverted, the new read-back fixtures observe
groomed marker bytes in place of the source; with the fix, they read
the original bytes. The fixtures groom the freed size class before
reading so the failure is deterministic, and electron.cjs now asserts
the three read-backs so the fallback path has coverage.

Also annotates the 3.12.3 changelog entry with the BufferSlice
security fix that shipped in it.

* test(napi): make from_external fallback fixtures deterministic via overwrite-in-finalizer

Address CodeRabbit review on #3503: recycling the freed chunk with
grooming allocations depended on allocator size-class behavior, so a
stale pointer could still observe the original bytes on some platforms.
The fixture finalizers now overwrite the source bytes with 0xFF before
freeing, so a stale slice deterministically fails to observe the
original contents regardless of allocator recycling. Verified on the
Electron lane: with the fix reverted the probes fail with freed-memory
garbage, with the fix they pass.

fix(napi): validate wrapped payload provenance in Object::unwrap/remove_wrapped (#3506)

* fix(napi): validate wrapped object identity via type tags in Object::unwrap/remove_wrapped

Object::wrap/Env::wrap attach a TaggedObject<T> payload, but
unwrap/remove_wrapped trusted the layout of whatever pointer
napi_unwrap returned: for objects not produced by those APIs (e.g.
#[napi] class instances, which wrap a bare pointer) the in-memory
TypeId read inspected bytes that are not a TaggedObject header, and
remove_wrapped detached the wrap (stripping its finalizer) before
discovering a type mismatch.

On napi8-native builds, wrap now stamps the object with a per-type
wrap tag (object_wrap_type_tag, namespaced under napi::object_wrap::
so it cannot collide with class content-hash tags), and
unwrap/remove_wrapped verify it via napi_check_object_type_tag before
touching the payload. The in-memory TypeId comparison is kept -- it
still disambiguates same-named types from different crate versions --
and remains the only check on pre-napi8 / wasm builds (unchanged
behavior there).

remove_wrapped/drop_wrapped now validate before calling
napi_remove_wrap, so a type mismatch leaves the wrap and its finalizer
intact, and a null payload is rejected instead of dereferenced. wrap
rolls back (remove_wrap + free) if stamping fails, accepting an
already-present matching tag so re-wrapping after remove_wrapped keeps
working. The same shared logic covers the compat-mode Env::unwrap /
Env::drop_wrapped twins.

* fix(napi): track wrapped object payloads in a registry for unwrap validation

Replace the type-tag stamping from the previous commit: N-API type tags
cannot be replaced or cleared once set, so a tag left behind by
remove_wrapped would still match after the same JS object acquired a
different payload (e.g. a #[napi] class payload wrapped by a constructor
callback running with an existing this).

Object::wrap/Env::wrap now record each payload pointer in a
process-local registry (mirroring the AbortSignal stack registry in
task.rs); unwrap/remove_wrapped and the compat-mode Env twins accept
only registered pointers, which proves this binary wrapped the payload
and that it was not detached or finalized since -- before any in-memory
TypeId read. The registry is pure Rust state, so the check works on
every N-API version and on wasm, and re-wrapping an object with a
different type after remove_wrapped works again. The in-memory TypeId
comparison stays to pin down T among registered payloads. Entries are
removed by remove_wrapped/drop_wrapped and by the wrap finalizer, which
now deregisters before freeing so the registry never outlives the
allocation.

Class type-tag machinery (tag_object/validate_type_tag, receiver and
accessor checks) is unchanged.

fix(cli): never wedge reconciliation locks when host identity probes fail (#3521)

Fixes #3512.

The reconciliation lock owner JSON is built from host execution-identity
probes that shell out to reg.exe / powershell.exe on Windows under a hard
2s timeout that silently resolves to null. On fresh CI VMs (slow first
powershell start) the owner was published with null machine/boot, and
processOwnerState fails closed on such owners by design: never stale,
never reclaimable, so the first orphaned lock wedged every later
acquisition and the build died after a 5s wait with
reconciliationOwnerCannotBeVerifiedError. Retries could never help.

- Acquisition now resolves a complete execution identity before writing
  anything, re-probing within a 10s budget; owners (lock and reclaim)
  are only ever published with complete machine/boot/namespace identity.
- Hosts that cannot provide identity (FreeBSD, containers without
  /etc/machine-id, policy-blocked Windows tools) degrade to lock-free
  operation with a warning when uncontended, preserving pre-3.8.0
  behavior instead of failing. An existing lock is still respected
  fail-closed and never bypassed; if it outlives the acquisition
  deadline the build fails with an actionable EAGAIN error naming the
  missing identity components.
- Degraded acquisitions skip transaction-journal recovery and sibling
  scavenging: recovery assumes cross-process exclusivity and could
  otherwise roll back a live transaction. Leftover journals still fail
  later publishes loudly and are recovered by the next run whose probes
  succeed.
- The degraded wait re-reads identity every iteration and transitions
  to normal acquisition (including stale-lock reclaim) once probes
  recover; a 30s memo makes one build pay the probe-failure wait once.
- One-shot host identity probes (win32 reg/powershell, darwin
  ioreg/sysctl) get a 15s timeout so slow first-start tools on fresh CI
  VMs actually answer; per-PID incarnation probes keep 2s.

processOwnerState's fail-closed reclamation policy, lock placement, the
5s cleanup timeout, and journal formats are unchanged.

fix(cli): run the wasm env cleanup barrier on a raw emnapi `Context.destroy()` (#3514)

* fix(cli): run the wasm env cleanup barrier on a raw emnapi `Context.destroy()`

`Context.destroy()` disables JavaScript calls before it runs its cleanup hooks,
and the threadsafe function's hook then drains its queue with a null env, so a
destroy that skips `napi_prepare_wasm_env_cleanup` strands exactly the promises
the barrier exists to cancel and deliver. The loaders ordered that correctly on
their own disposal paths only; an embedder holding the context, a test harness,
or emnapi's `beforeExit` auto-destroy reached `destroy()` without the barrier.

Every generated loader now shadows `destroy` on the context it creates, so the
ordering is owned by the object instead of by each call site.

Shadowing `destroy` makes the barrier reachable from inside itself, so the
barrier had to become reentrancy-aware. `napi_prepare_wasm_env_cleanup` settles
the promises it cancels synchronously, while the Rust side holds a
non-reentrant lifecycle mutex, and V8 runs promise hooks synchronously too: a
`promiseHooks.onSettled` handler — or the `async_hooks` hook
`AsyncLocalStorage` installs — that calls `destroy()` re-enters the wrapper from
inside the barrier, and a second trip into the export aborts the wasm instance
with `cannot recursively acquire mutex`. The in-flight flag lives in the barrier
rather than in the wrapper, so it also covers `dispose()`, which runs the
barrier before it ever calls `destroy()`. While a prepare is in flight a nested
`destroy()` returns without running either the barrier or the real destroy: the
frame that started the barrier destroys the moment it returns, still
synchronously, and `Context.destroy()` is typed `void`, so nothing observable is
lost. Letting it through instead tears the environment down mid-barrier and
strands every settlement the barrier had not reached yet.

* fix(cli): coalesce reentrant disposal in the deferred WASI loader

The nested-destroy no-op added with the teardown barrier rests on one
assumption: the frame that started the barrier destroys the moment the
barrier returns, still synchronously. The deferred loader's instance
`dispose()` is the one frame that does not. It runs the barrier and then
yields for the settlement drain before it reaches the context destroyer.

The barrier settles the promises it cancels synchronously, so a promise
hook can run while the first `dispose()` is parked in that drain. A hook
that calls the same instance's `dispose()` again started a second frame:
it found the barrier flagged in flight, prepared nothing, drained
nothing, and went straight to the managed destroyer, whose
`Context.destroy()` was the wrapper's no-op. The destroyer recorded that
as a completed destroy, so when the outer frame finished its drain it
skipped the real one. Both disposal promises resolved, no cleanup hook
ran, and the context stayed retained.

The instance now publishes its disposal promise before any of that
starts, exactly like the eager loaders' `__disposeWasiBinding`, so a
reentrant caller joins the disposal already running instead of racing it.
A failed disposal still clears the memo, so a drain that rejected stays
retryable. As a backstop for any other caller that reaches the managed
destroyer from inside the barrier, the destroyer now refuses instead of
flagging a destroy it never performed.

fix(cli): bound symlink-ancestor reconciliation guards to the anchor's parent (#3522)

Refs #3444.

The lock-identity walk keyed every symlink component of the requested
path that had a writable parent, and placed each guard lock at
realpath(dirname(component)). A symlinked top-level component (e.g. a
symlinked mount point in a root-run container, where the filesystem
root is writable) therefore scattered
.napi-rs-filesystem-reconciliation.<hash>.swp locks into arbitrary
ancestors, up to /.

Symlink-component guards are now kept only where their lock root stays
within the anchor's parent, and each accepted guard's lock root is
resolved once at walk time and carried into the identity, so the
containment-checked root is the root the lock is created under (no
double-resolution race). Topology swaps remain fail-safe: the anchor
and requested-path assertions still re-stat dev/ino and throw ESTALE,
and the canonical anchor guard plus object-identity lock already make
processes converge on the same lock set regardless of path spelling.

The deliberate placement of the anchor guard and object lock in the
anchor's immediate parent is unchanged: those locks must sit outside
the guarded tree to survive the anchor being renamed or retired
mid-transaction.

feat(cli): export `__napiBindingTarget` from generated binding loaders (#3515)

* feat(cli): export `__napiBindingTarget` from generated binding loaders

Every generated loader now reports which artifact actually loaded: `'native'`
for a `.node` addon, otherwise the `platformArchABI` of the WASI flavor
(`'wasm32-wasi'` threaded, `'wasm32-wasip1'` threadless). The root loader
tracks it across the native path and the whole WASI fallback chain; each
flavor's CommonJS, browser and deferred `./workerd` loader exports its own
fixed identity. Consumers had no supported way to branch on native vs.
WebAssembly and resorted to post-processing the emitted loaders.

The marker travels on the binding object each loader hands out, not only as a
module export, so the browser loader's default export, `instantiate()`'s result
and `createInstance().exports` answer it the way their declarations promise.
`NAPI_RS_NATIVE_LIBRARY_PATH` may point at a generated WASI loader, so the root
entry adopts the target the required module reports instead of assuming
`'native'` and overwriting that loader's marker through the alias.

With type generation on, the export is declared in the generated `.d.ts` as a
literal union of the flavors that package can produce, and a napi export named
`__napiBindingTarget` is now rejected at build time.

* fix(cli): declare the binding target exactly when a loader is written

`__napiBindingTarget` exists only on a generated loader, so a declaration
file should carry it when — and only when — this build writes one. Two
sides of that switch were wrong, and they are one decision:

- A crate that registers every export from a `#[napi(module_exports)]`
  hook emits no `.type` file. `generateTypeDef` returned early for it,
  before the declaration was appended, so the loader written for that
  crate exported `__napiBindingTarget` while its `index.d.ts` (and the
  `.d.cts` derived from it) stayed empty — `import { __napiBindingTarget }`
  failed to compile against a loader that does export it.
- A merely *configured* WASI flavor made the old `emitsLoader` true. A
  non-WASI build only regenerates the flavors whose previous loader
  metadata is still on disk and skips the rest, and `writeJsBinding`
  writes nothing without `--platform`, with `--no-js-binding`, or with no
  exports and no WASI fallback. Those builds leave a raw `.node` and an
  `index.d.ts` declaring an export nothing defines.

Fixing only the first reintroduces the second on the empty-typedef path,
so both now go through one predicate,
`bindingTargetDeclarationPredicate`, which mirrors the two writers:

    declare = emitsWasiLoader
              || (rootLoaderCandidate && (hasWasiFallback || exports > 0))

`exports` is known only after typegen runs, and typegen writes
`index.d.ts` itself before either writer is called, so
`declareBindingTarget` accepts a predicate over the generated export
list instead of a flag decided up front. `willEmitWasiLoader` asks
whether a flavor's loader will really be rewritten rather than whether
one is configured; it probes `finalOutputDir`, which the staging swap
never touches, so it sees exactly what `writeWasiBinding` will.

The root declaration keeps the full union: `NAPI_RS_NATIVE_LIBRARY_PATH`
can point the root loader at any flavor, and a WASI `.d.cts` still
derives from `index.d.ts` before being narrowed to its own literal —
which is why a `--target wasm32-wasip1` build with no `--platform` still
declares it.

Verified against a fake-cargo build matrix: the four shapes that declared
an undefined export (no `--platform` with a configured flavor,
`--platform --no-js-binding`, `--platform` with zero runtime exports, and
a configured flavor with zero exports) now declare nothing, while
`--platform` builds and builds over existing WASI loaders are byte-for-byte
unchanged. `examples/napi` regenerates identically.

* fix(cli): stamp the binding target without clobbering or throwing

Four generated loaders wrote `__napiBindingTarget` straight onto an exports
object they do not own — the addon's own object, which the root CJS loader
aliases and which emnapi hands back from `instantiateNapiModule`. A
`#[napi(module_exports)]` hook can have already shaped that object, and the
bare assignment got both cases wrong:

- The hook may have claimed the name. `assertBindingTargetIdentFree` cannot
  see that: it reads the type-def export list, and a hook attaches names
  imperatively in Rust with no `.type` file behind them. The addon's value was
  silently destroyed, which contradicts the reservation the loader's own error
  text claims.
- The hook may have sealed or frozen it (`Object::seal` / `Object::freeze`).
  The deferred `./workerd` loader is ESM, so its assignment threw a TypeError
  inside the try block that flips `__lifecycleState` to 'failed' — a
  successful instantiation torn down over a metadata marker. (The eager
  browser and node loaders already required an extensible exports object one
  line earlier, in `__publishWasiDispose`; that is untouched here.)

Both are the same statement at four sites, so they get one emitted helper.
`__napiStampBindingTarget` checks `Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty` before any
mutation, in this order: same value already there is a no-op; a different value
throws with `code: 'ERR_NAPI_BINDING_TARGET_CONFLICT'`; a non-extensible object
with no collision is skipped, leaving the loader's module-level export as the
source of truth; otherwise it stamps.

The equal-value short circuit is load-bearing, not cosmetic. The root loader
adopts an override's reported flavor and then stamps the very object it read it
from, and every WASI fallback candidate arrives already carrying its flavor.
`Object.defineProperty` is not an alternative for the sealed case: it throws
there too, so it is strictly harder to satisfy than an assignment.

The contract moves to `templates/binding-target.ts` so both templates can emit
the same helper source. `load-wasi-template.ts` had no top-level imports, so the
shared module sits below both and the graph stays acyclic. The doc comment on
`assertBindingTargetIdentFree` now states what it actually covers — type-def
reported exports — mirroring how `typeDefAvailable` documents the same blind
spot; the assertion and both call sites are unchanged.

Behaviour change: a package whose addon already exports `__napiBindingTarget`
from a hook used to load with the value replaced, and now throws at require
time. That is the guarantee the reservation already claimed.

* fix(cli): keep __napiBindingTarget a static CommonJS export and stamp WASI loaders inside the rollback boundary

Routing the four stamps through `__napiStampBindingTarget` replaced two
statically visible assignments with bare calls, and each bare call broke
something the assignment had been carrying.

**The named export stopped existing.** Node's CJS -> ESM named export detection
is `cjs-module-lexer`, a static scanner: it reports `__napiBindingTarget` only
when it can read a `module.exports.<name> =` assignment out of the source. A
bare call is invisible to it, so `import { __napiBindingTarget } from
'<package>'` no longer linked at all — a hard `SyntaxError: Named export
'__napiBindingTarget' not found` on `index.cjs`, `example.wasi.cjs` and
`example.wasip1.cjs` alike. No test caught it because every existing consumer
goes through `require()`.

The guard now returns `target` from each of its three non-throwing branches and
the two CommonJS emit sites assign that return value. This relies on the
generated CommonJS loaders being sloppy mode, which they are — none of them
emits `'use strict'`. On a frozen exports object the guard skips and the
assignment is a silent no-op instead of a `TypeError`, so a frozen addon keeps
loading and the named import links to `undefined` rather than failing. The
alternative shape the lexer also detects, `Object.defineProperty`, throws on a
sealed or frozen object, so it is strictly harder to satisfy than an assignment.

**A WASI conflict stopped rolling back.** In the node CommonJS WASI loader the
stamp is appended by `build.ts`, past the end of the initialization `try`. A
`#[napi(module_exports)]` hook that claims the name makes the guard throw
`ERR_NAPI_BINDING_TARGET_CONFLICT` from outside that boundary, so the catch that
runs `__rollbackWasiInitialization` never sees it: the emnapi context stayed
built and the process `'exit'` listener stayed installed. Three failed requires
left three contexts and three exit listeners, and the root loader's fallback
loop swallows the candidate error and moves on, so the process carries an
initialized WASI environment nothing can reach. The browser and deferred ESM
loaders already stamped inside their try; only this one was outside.

The template now stamps `__napiModule.exports` right after
`__publishWasiDispose`, mirroring the browser template, and `build.ts` keeps its
appended line purely for the lexer — `module.exports` aliases the object the
loader already stamped, so the guard returns the same value there (or skips a
frozen one).

e19aff25 moved a stamp into the node WASI loader's initialization `try` but left
the appended tail stamp in place, so two guarded stamps ran — the second past
the boundary. Two things still escaped it.

**A marker changed after the first stamp.** `__installCurrentThreadHosts` hands
`__napiModule.exports` to addon-provided registration functions, which run after
the in-try stamp. If one of them puts the reserved name on that object, the tail
guard sees a different own value and throws `ERR_NAPI_BINDING_TARGET_CONFLICT`

host registrations and the `'exit'` listener all survive the failed `require()`.
Measured on the real threadless artifact: two attempts, two leaked listeners.

**An accessor whose setter refuses writes.** `Object::define_property` in a
`#[napi(module_exports)]` hook can expose a getter returning the very value the
loader is about to stamp. Both guard calls then return without writing — but the
tail is an *assignment*, and an assignment invokes a setter even in sloppy mode.
Confirmed against 00d56ab4: that shape loaded cleanly there, and leaked here.

So there is now exactly one stamp, and it sits after `${installAsyncRuntimeHosts}`
and before `__registerWasiExitListener()`, inside the `try`. It stamps

against any accessor — while assigning the return value onto the loader's own
`module.exports`, which is still the original object at that point. The addon's
object is never assigned through, so a refusing setter cannot be reached, and
the harmless property on the soon-to-be-replaced object is what
`cjs-module-lexer` reads. `build.ts` appends no executable stamp at all any more.

The lexer shape was verified before relying on it: an assignment inside a `try`
followed later by `module.exports = __napiModule.exports` is still detected as a
named export on node 20.20.2, 22.23.2 and 24 — the later reassignment does not

Every wasm build links with `--import-memory`, so the loader — not the module —

fallback chain reduces to today's single value, so generated output is

fix(cli): settle threaded WASI disposal after async work (#3526)

* fix(cli): terminate WASI pool workers through the thread manager on dispose

`@emnapi/wasi-threads` records a worker exit as expected only when its own
`ThreadManager.terminateWorker` performed the termination. The generated
threaded loaders called `worker.terminate()` directly, so the manager's
`exit` listener saw Node's normal terminate exit code 1, reported
`worker (tid = N) sent an error! Worker stopped with exit code 1` and rethrew
inside the emit. That throw aborts the emit, so the `once('exit')` backing the
terminate promise never runs: `dispose()` waits on a promise that can no longer
settle, and the process dies with an uncaught exception whenever something else
holds the event loop open.

One `napi_async_work` call followed by one `dispose()` is the whole trigger.
Sync-only calls never spawn a pool worker, and no example disposes a threaded
binding after async work, which is why no lane caught it.

Mark the termination on the manager first, then terminate. Not
`terminateAllThreads()`: its `shutdownAllWorkers(recreatePool = true)` spawns a
fresh pool in the middle of disposal.

* fix(cli): keep the event loop alive until WASI worker termination settles

The Node.js threaded loader unreferences its pool workers and stubs out the
`ref` functions on their `kHandle` / `kPublicPort` handles, so an idle binding
cannot hold the process open. `Worker#terminate()` references the worker
through exactly those two functions, to observe the 'exit' that resolves its
promise — so with them stubbed the pending terminations could not keep the loop
alive. An `await dispose()` with nothing else pending never resolved: the
process exited 0 with the promise still pending and everything after the
`await` skipped.

Keep the original `ref` functions when the stubs are installed and put them
back before terminating. Nothing has to unreference them again afterwards: the
worker is gone once the termination settles, and a termination that throws
synchronously unreferences the worker again so the process can still exit.

waiting-request counter balance through exactly the same path an ordinary

settled and `Task::finally` never ran.

The task promise is absent from that list entirely, and the leak warning is the
`finally` hook that never ran to unref the object.

entry with a guard whose `Drop` removes it, so every one of the several `?` paths

drain wait forever for a work that already completed — and drop it explicitly
just before `napi_delete_async_work` frees the handle, so a cancel sweep can
never be handed a dangling one.

instead, and still terminates: the poll is a timer, so it cannot run until the
callback has returned to the host, by which time the guard has dropped and the
entry is gone. `__disposeWasiBinding` hands every caller the same in-flight
promise, so the nested call joins that disposal rather than starting a second
one. Both points are now stated in the loader prelude.

* fix(cli): retry a filesystem snapshot whose source only changed metadata and name the drifted fields

`snapshotFileSystemTransactionInput` re-stats its source after the copy and
threw a single message for eight independent conditions — dev, ino, size,
bytes-read, mode, mtimeNs, ctimeNs and path identity — naming none of them.

Two consequences, both hit by rolldown's FreeBSD release build (see
rolldown/rolldown#10268), where `napi build --release --target
x86_64-unknown-freebsd` failed twice on the cli's own staged
`rolldown-binding.freebsd-x64.node` inside its own mkdtemp directory:

1. The report was undiagnosable. A truncated read, a chmod, a timestamp
   re-stamp and a replaced path are the same string, so a failure from a
   platform the author cannot reach carries no signal.
2. A metadata-only re-stamp failed a release build. A kernel or a permission
   normalization can move ctime/mtime/mode without touching a byte, and the
   snapshot's job is a consistent *copy*, which the recorded sha256 plus
   dev/ino/size already guarantee.

Classify the drift instead. Hard fields (dev, ino, size, bytes-read, path
identity) stay fatal on first observation. Soft fields (mode, mtimeNs,
ctimeNs) on an otherwise identical inode redo the copy into the same
transaction-owned destination, up to 3 attempts; the source descriptor is
deliberately not re-opened, so a retry can never adopt a successor swapped
into the path, and a genuinely torn write keeps moving mtime until the bound
is spent and still throws. Either way the message now lists every field that
moved with its before and after value, behind the original prefix.

Reproduced on macOS against the real `commitFileSystemTransaction`: a single
transient same-mode chmod during the copy of a 20,982,240-byte source fails
3/3 runs before this change and passes 3/3 after.

* test(cli): make the snapshot drift tests platform-aware

The Windows lanes run `yarn test:cli` (`.github/workflows/test-release.yaml`,
`windows-latest` and `windows-11-arm`), and four of the new snapshot drift
tests were written against POSIX-only filesystem semantics. On
x86_64-pc-windows-msvc node@22 they failed:

* two tests forced drift with an identical-mode `chmod`, expecting it to
  advance `ctime`. On Windows that is an attribute no-op — both observed
  `attempts` of `[1]` and no throw, i.e. no drift at all.
* the mode test asserted a literal `0o640` and got `0o666`. Node documents
  that on Windows "only the write permission can be changed, and the
  distinction among the permissions of group, owner, or others is not
  implemented", and libuv reports exactly `0o444` when FILE_ATTRIBUTE_READONLY
  is set and `0o666` otherwise.
* the path-replacement test renamed a successor over a path the snapshot still
  holds open, which Windows refuses:
  `EPERM: operation not permitted, rename '...\successor.node' -> '...\source.node'`.

Force timestamp drift with `utimes` instead, moving `mtime` to a whole second.
`mtime` is defined to change on every supported platform and is the field
libuv fills from LastWriteTime, so the mutation is deterministic everywhere —
no sleeping, no racing. The mode test now toggles only the owner write bit,
the one transition Windows can represent, and asserts against the mode the
platform actually reports rather than a literal; it also asserts that the
transition produced real drift so it cannot pass vacuously.

The two mutations with no Windows equivalent — an identical-mode `chmod` for
ctime-only drift, and replacing a path with a live handle — keep their
original assertions and are gated to POSIX with the reason at each site. All
six behaviors stay covered, and both drift classes still run on Windows: the
soft-drift retry through `utimes` and the hard-field fatality through the
size-change test.

* fix(cli): require a stable content hash before a retried snapshot is accepted

The metadata-drift retry added in the previous commit rebases its baseline on
the stats it just observed and keeps only the newest attempt's hash. That is
enough while a timestamp moves on every write, but a timestamp only moves as
far as its filesystem can express it. On a coarse clock, or when several writes
land inside one tick, a writer that rewrites the file in place at the same
length moves nothing the snapshot compares: dev, ino, size, bytes-read, mode
and both timestamps all match the rebased baseline. The retry would then accept
a copy that mixed two versions of the file and record that mixture's hash as
the authoritative one. Nothing later re-reads the source, so the torn image
could be prepared and published.

A retry now has to reproduce the bytes as well as the metadata: an attempt that
follows drift is accepted only when its hash equals the hash of the attempt
before it, so two consecutive passes have to agree before the snapshot is
taken as settled. A hash that keeps changing is named as `contentHash` drift
and spends the attempt bound like any other field, which leaves the error one
shape. A benign re-stamp still costs exactly one extra attempt, because the
next pass reads the same bytes.

Reported in review of napi-rs/napi-rs#3530.

fix(napi): validate native payload provenance for External and instance data (#3540)

* fix(napi): validate native payload provenance for External and instance data

napi_get_value_external and napi_get_instance_data hand back untyped data
pointers, and the JS values / env slots they hang off can be populated by
foreign native code -- another addon, or a sibling copy of this crate --
carrying arbitrary payload pointers. The previous validation read the
payload's in-memory TypeId header before knowing the pointer was ours,
which dereferences potentially invalid memory (CodeQL
rust/access-invalid-pointer).

Switch to payload provenance, the same pattern Object::wrap/unwrap uses
for napi_wrap payloads: a process-local registry records every live
payload this binary creates, keyed by pointer with the payload's TypeId
as value, and readers accept only registered pointers. The registry keys
on the pointer alone, so the check is pure Rust state and works on every
N-API version and on wasm; since the marker carries the expected payload
type, no in-memory header read is needed at all.

- External<T>::from_raw_impl and ExternalRef::from_napi_value now share
  one helper gated on registry membership; the same registration covers
  the deprecated Env::create_external/get_value_external pair, which
  register and check TaggedObject<T> markers instead so cross-kind
  confusion between External<T> and TaggedObject<T> payloads is rejected
  too
- Env::set_instance_data/get_instance_data validate through the same
  registry; the instance-data payload becomes a repr(C) struct so the
  TaggedObject<T> field is guaranteed to sit at offset zero
- set_instance_finalize_callback and a new finalize_external_payload
  deregister payloads before freeing them
- failed napi_create_external/napi_set_instance_data calls now drop the
  boxed payload and hint instead of leaking them

* docs(async-runtime): state the rules for MultiThread on threaded WASI

Everything a host has to know that the type signatures do not say:

* Pass a worker count. `available_parallelism()` answers Ok(1) inside a
  WASI host, so flipping only the flavor lands on the clamped minimum of
  two workers and one blocking lane. The crate never probes the CPU
  count on wasm; the host reads it in JavaScript.
* Peak threads are `worker_threads + 1` -- the first `sleep_until`
  lazily spawns a timekeeper thread, one more Node Worker.
* Route through `try_spawn` / `try_spawn_blocking` / `try_block_on_dyn`.
  Pool construction is lazy, so the first async call is what calls
  `wasi.thread-spawn`; these return the failure instead of panicking.

  barrier and worker join all park on `memory.atomic.wait32`, which
  emnapi answers with `napi_would_deadlock` there.
* Panics abort. Both WASI targets are `panic = "abort"`, so the
  crate's containment never catches anything; MultiThread only widens
  that surface to every worker plus the timekeeper.
* `shutdown` joins without a bound, inside a synchronous wasm export on
  the loader path. A bounded join would be worse -- a live thread over
  memory the loader is about to destroy.
