* fix(napi): settle cross-thread cancel rejections on the JS thread during wasm env cleanup

On `wasm32-wasip1-threads` a backend's `shutdown` can drop a cancelled task on
one of its own worker threads (the `napi-async-runtime` crate's MultiThread
flavor routinely does, and its shutdown joins those workers, so the drop
precedes the shutdown call's return). The task's `Drop` then rejects its
`JsDeferred` from that worker, where the environment-cleanup thread-local reads
zero and the deferred's owner is another thread — so the settle can only go into
the threadsafe-function queue, which `@emnapi/core` dispatches from a macrotask
two turns later. A host that calls the raw, synchronous `Context.destroy()`
never gets there: `destroy()` disables JavaScript calls first and then runs the
threadsafe function's cleanup hook, which drains the queue with a null env and
discards the item. The promise never settles.

`napi_prepare_wasm_env_cleanup` now opens a cancel mailbox before the backend
shutdown and drains it right after that shutdown returns, while the
`WasmEnvCleanupBarrier` guard is still alive. A cancellation raised off the
barrier thread is parked instead of invoked; replaying it on the JavaScript
thread inside the barrier makes it settle synchronously, exactly as the
threadless `wasm32-wasip1` artifact has always behaved. Taking the vector out
under the lock is also the close, so a deposit that races the drain falls
through to today's queue path — the current behaviour, never worse. Moving the
callback across threads is sound by its own bound: both
`AsyncRuntimeTaskCancelCallback` and `Error` are `Send + 'static`.

Native builds are unchanged: every new item is gated on `target_family =
"wasm"`, and `invoke_cancel_callback` keeps its old body verbatim under a new
name.

The custom-async-runtime example gains a parked-task worker thread on threaded
WASI (`parkNextSpawnOnWorker()` / `parkedTasksOnWorker()`). It is the only way
this example can own a task on a thread that is not the JavaScript thread — it
polls tasks inline and runs blocking work inline everywhere else on wasm.
`test.mjs` uses it for the threaded counterpart of the existing raw
`Context.destroy()` case: without the mailbox the promise stays `PENDING`, with

`test-custom-async-runtime-wasi-threads` mirrors its `wasm32-wasip1` sibling
with the threaded target (no wasi-sdk needed; the CLI ships the emnapi archives

* feat(async-runtime): split shutdown into begin/finish phases with a work-pending poll

`shutdown` does begin_shutdown + wait_until_idle + join + `Stopped` in one
synchronous call. On the threaded WASI artifact that call is entered from the
JS thread, which is also the only thread that can give a running blocking
closure the JS turn it is waiting for -- so it waits for work that can never
finish. Split it so the host can yield in between:

  begin_shutdown() -> Result<bool, _>   publish the stop, close admission,
                                        abort tasks, drop queued work,
                                        drain-fire timers, wake parkers --
                                        never waits. true = work still live
  runtime_work_pending() -> bool        non-blocking poll for that window
  finish_shutdown() -> Result<(), _>    wait_until_idle + join + `Stopped`
  shutdown()                            begin_shutdown()? + finish_shutdown()

Invariant: `shutdown` is unchanged. Phase 1 ends at
`RuntimeBackend::begin_shutdown` and phase 2 resumes at `wait_until_idle`,
with nothing in between, so the ordering, the five lifecycle arms, the
stop-publication order and the self-deadlock guards are the same code on the
same path. `RuntimeState` gains a `draining` slot because `Stopping` carries
only an identity: the backend used to live on `shutdown`'s stack, and the
split needs somewhere to park it across the host's yield window.

Re-entrancy: a `begin_shutdown` while one is outstanding starts no second
phase and never waits -- it re-reports `runtime_work_pending`, so the thread
that owns the shutdown may call it again from a host turn. Only
`finish_shutdown` waits, which keeps a cross-thread `shutdown` blocking
exactly as it does today. Admission needs no new code: `backend_locked`
already rejects every submission under `Stopping`. `start` between the phases
is not allowed and the docs say so.

`runtime_work_pending` composes the non-blocking reads of the three
predicates `wait_until_idle` sleeps on. Joining the workers is deliberately
not one of them: a Rayon worker exits when the last backend handle is
dropped, which only phase 2 does, so a worker count would never answer false
in the window -- and that join waits on thread teardown, never on user work.

reports the closure instead of waiting, a submission in the window is
rejected, the poll goes false once it retires, phase 2 stops and a restart
still works), a concurrent single-call `shutdown` during a handshake, a
re-entered phase 1, the CurrentThread/threadless shape, and an orphan phase 2.

* feat(napi): expose the two-phase wasm env cleanup to the loader

`napi_prepare_wasm_env_cleanup` waits: it returns only once the backend has
quiesced, and on `wasm32-wasip1-threads` the thread it waits on is the same
JavaScript thread a running blocking closure may be waiting for a turn from, so
it waits for work that can never finish. Split the export so a loader can put
real event-loop turns in the middle:

  napi_prepare_wasm_env_cleanup_begin() -> u32   open the cancel mailbox, latch
                                                 the disposal, raise the
                                                 barrier, backend phase 1.
                                                 1 = work is still live
  napi_wasm_runtime_work_pending() -> u32        non-blocking poll for that
                                                 window; 0 = finish will not
                                                 block. Safe at any time
  napi_prepare_wasm_env_cleanup_finish()         backend phase 2 (this is the
                                                 call that joins), drain the
                                                 mailbox, lower the barrier

`napi_prepare_wasm_env_cleanup` keeps its name and is now exactly
`begin(); finish();` -- byte for byte the sequence it always ran, with nothing
between the halves. Every shipped loader and the `process.on('exit')` path is
unchanged, and a loader feature-detects the new names the same way it already
feature-detects this one.

A latch makes the pair idempotent the way the single call is: a second `begin`
re-reports the poll and starts no second teardown, and a `finish` with no
`begin` outstanding tears nothing down and lowers no barrier. Module
registration clears it, for the same reason it releases the disposal latch.

The barrier is what makes a cancelled task's rejection settle its promise
directly instead of queueing it for a dispatch a synchronous `Context.destroy()`
never reaches, so it has to span both phases -- including the host's turns, where
a threaded backend's own cancellations land. A guard scoped to one Rust stack
frame cannot do that when each phase is a separate export that returns to
JavaScript, so `WasmEnvCleanupBarrier` becomes an explicit
`enter_wasm_env_cleanup_barrier` / `leave_wasm_env_cleanup_barrier` pair on the
same thread-local depth counter. Both wasm targets build `panic = "abort"`, so
no unwind path can skip the lowering.

* fix(cli): make the cleanup poll stall backup rescue every parked turn

The backup that ends a runtime-work poll turn whose timer never arrives
judged by elapsed time, behind a throttle: an arm was skipped unless the
last one was a stall window old, and at fire time it only ended a turn

armed at `a` fires at `a + 2w` and could only rescue a turn parked at

past the throttle and closed the gap between the two; at one-millisecond
turns the margin was about a millisecond, so it flaked.

read next to the arming they describe, and a backup ends a parked turn
only when that turn's own timer came due a whole window before this
backup did - hosts run timers in due order, so a backup that runs anyway
proves the timer was dropped rather than delayed, and a healthy turn has
already run and cleared itself before any later backup can look. Arming
every turn makes the backup that covers a parked turn the one the turn
before it armed, so nothing depends on how far apart the arms fall; what
is left of the backup's own wait, after the window and one interval, is
the ceiling on a single poll turn.

A turn now clears `settleTurn` when it ends, so a backup can no longer
read a due time that turn has already answered.

* fix(async-runtime): pair every opened shutdown phase with exactly one finish

`shutdown` is `begin_shutdown` + `finish_shutdown`, so it takes the lifecycle
lock twice. On an already stopped (or `Initial`) runtime phase 1 settles with
no backend and publishes no `Stopping` for a `start` to wait in, so a `start`
from another thread can land in that window. It drops the parked handoff --
correctly, a stale handoff must never answer for the new generation -- and
phase 2 then found an empty slot with a `Running` lifecycle and reported "the
async runtime shutdown was not started" for a shutdown the call had really
performed. Running the two affected tests 100x natively failed 15 times
(`stopped_shutdown_blocks_restart_until_rejected_destruction_retires`,
`failed_initial_submission_destruction_blocks_retry_and_shutdown`); on
`wasm32-wasip1-threads`, where `panic = abort` kills the binary, it aborted the
whole lane 3-5 runs in 10.

The `draining` slot cannot answer phase 2 on its own, because two different
threads empty it: whoever reaches phase 2 first TAKES it, and a `start` DROPS
it. `phase_one_begun: bool` could not separate those either -- a `start`
cleared it, which is what turned a completed shutdown into an error.

Replace the flag with `outstanding_phases: u32`, a count of openings not yet
paired with a consuming finish:

- `open_phase_one` (every `begin_shutdown` arm that parks a handoff, `Backend`
  or `Settled`) increments it. A `begin_shutdown` that only re-reports an
  already outstanding handoff opens nothing and counts nothing.
- `start` (and `backend_locked`'s lazy first backend) drops the handoff and
  leaves the count alone. Dropping `draining` answers the stale-handoff
  question completely; a `start` cannot cancel a pairing whose owner is still
  holding it.
- `finish_shutdown` gains an internal `consume` flag. The public call passes
  `true`; `shutdown` passes whether ITS phase 1 opened the phase, so it never
  pairs off a phase another thread opened. Both `Some(..)` arms decrement when
  consuming; with an empty slot the terminal arms answer `Ok(())` when the
  caller waited through the publication, or when it consumes and an opened
  phase is still unpaired, or when it opened nothing -- and only otherwise is
  it the orphan error.

* fix(async-runtime): make finish_shutdown idempotent instead of counting phases

The outstanding-phase count added in 52689bfb is race-prone by construction:
the credit is spent by whichever thread performs the join, not by the thread
that opened the phase. A concurrent in-protocol `begin_shutdown` +
`finish_shutdown` therefore pairs off a single-call `shutdown`'s own phase,
and that `shutdown` is then told "the async runtime shutdown was not started"
-- after it published the stop. A 100k-iteration probe over the public API hit
it in 8.2% of CurrentThread runs (1 in 300k on MultiThread, where the pool
join keeps the opener in the waiting branch). `(begin, start)` pairs also leak
credits that nothing ever drains, so k stray phase 2s later report success off
a leaked count.

Replace the count with the simplest model that cannot race: a single sticky
`RuntimeState::phase_ever_opened`, set by every `begin_shutdown` that opens a
phase and never cleared. `finish_shutdown` completes the most recently
announced stop and is idempotent -- it takes and drains a parked handoff,
waits out a join another thread is performing, and otherwise reports `Ok(())`.

nothing outstanding is a no-op. The only error left for a missing phase is
phase 2 on a runtime that has never begun a shutdown at all. `shutdown` is

is unchanged.

* fix(async-runtime): keep the joining backend visible until Stopped is published

`finish_shutdown` took the phase-1 handoff out of `draining` and only then
waited, so for the whole join the state read `draining = None` with the
lifecycle still `Stopping`. In that window a concurrent `begin_shutdown`
missed its outstanding-handoff arm, fell through to the lifecycle loop and
PARKED on `lifecycle_changed` until the join it was racing finished --
breaking the documented "a phase 1 while one is outstanding never waits"
contract -- and `runtime_work_pending` answered `false` about work the
finisher was demonstrably still waiting for. A host whose phase-1 call has to
come from the very thread the drained work needs deadlocks there.

Keep an explicit in-flight marker in the slot instead: the taker swaps the
handoff for `ShutdownDrain::Joining` and retires it under the same lock that
publishes `Stopped`, so no observer ever sees `Stopping` without a drain or
`Stopped` with one. The marker carries the backend only across
`wait_until_idle` -- the half that can still report work -- and drops it
before the drainer releases its own last reference, because that release is
what lets the executor go and the workers exit; a marker holding a clone
wedges `wait_for_all_workers` forever.

The outstanding-handoff arm returns before the retired-generation guard, and
this widens the window it covers to the whole join, so the guard moves ahead
of it: work of a retired generation is still told so instead of being handed
the current stop's verdict.

A second `finish_shutdown` during the join keeps today's behaviour (wait for
the publication, then `Ok(())`), `start` still waits out `Stopping` so
`forget_shutdown_handoff` only ever runs after the publication, and the
single call's ordering is unchanged.

* fix(async-runtime): keep phase 1 from waiting on rejected destructors

A Codex review of 3a5e12f2 found that two arms of `begin_shutdown` broke
the contract phase 1 was created to keep. On a runtime with no backend --
`Initial`, or one already stopped -- phase 1 published
`StoppingWithoutBackend` and then parked on `lifecycle_changed` until
`rejected_drops` reached zero. That count is held open by another
thread's user `Drop`: the rejecting thread runs the destructor of the
future it could not submit with the guard still live. So phase 1, which
every layer of this PR documents as "never waits", blocked on arbitrary
user code on a thread it does not control. On the threaded WASI artifact
that is a deadlock, not a stall: the loader calls `begin()` as a
synchronous wasm export, so a destructor waiting for a JavaScript turn
waits for a turn the blocked caller can only give by returning.

The wait now belongs to phase 2. A new `ShutdownDrain::ZeroBackend(target)`
handoff carries the announced stop: phase 1 publishes
`StoppingWithoutBackend(target)`, parks the handoff and returns
`Ok(true)` without waiting; `runtime_work_pending` reports
`rejected_drops != 0` for that handoff, which is what keeps the host
turning the loop the destructor needs; the outstanding-handoff arm of a
second phase 1 answers the same verdict under the lock; and
`finish_shutdown` does the wait and publishes the target under one lock
hold. The handoff is not taken the way `Backend` is, so that arm re-reads
the slot after each wake -- two concurrent finishers cannot both publish,
and `rejected_drops` flickering 1 -> 0 -> 1 across host turns is
re-observed rather than raced.

Everything else is left alone. The `Running` arm never waited and is
untouched, as is the phase-2 tail wait and its debug asserts, which the
new arm returns before reaching. `start()` needs no code change: it
already parks on `StoppingWithoutBackend` and already rejects a
drop-context caller, so widening that window to last until phase 2 is
what makes the zero-backend path behave like the backend path. Every
`RejectedSubmissionDropContext::is_current()` guard is kept, including
the one in the `Initial` arm that stops a destructor from re-entering its
own shutdown. `shutdown()` stays net-identical: same blocking time, same
result, same final state.

Three tests pin it, each driving the call that would hang from a spawned
thread behind a `recv_timeout` so a regression fails instead of wedging
the suite. Rustdoc, the crate README and the napi export doc are updated
in the same change: `Ok(true)` now also means "a rejected submission is
still being destroyed".

Reduce need for server restarts (#2111)

* Reduce need for server restarts

Reduce (nearly remove) the need for server restart when adding/updating/removing routes, data buckets, etc. by making the server more dynamic and regenerating/enabling features when the server is already running, notably:
- making the routing more dynamic by using a wildcard endpoint and matching the routes at runtime, rather than creating routes during server start. For this, we directly use path-to-regexp in its latest version (8) with a compatibility layer to stay backward compatible with most of express 4 path syntax. As a result, regexes are no longer supported (it's a tradeoff to be able to use the safer latest version).
- regenerating/deleting data buckets live.
- enabling/disabling the proxy and updating its target live.
- starting and stopping WS servers when they are created/deleted/updated.
- enabling/disabling routes locally is also propagated to the server and applied live.

Some environment properties still requires a restart locally: port, hostname, etc.

Other changes: stop emitting the create-proxy event as the proxy is always created but only used at runtime if it is enabled and the URL valid.

additions while maintaining full test coverage for proxy response headers.
